The Atacama Desert is a desert plateau in South America, located mainly in northern Chile and extending in places toward southern Peru. It is often described as the driest non-polar desert in the world, and some weather stations in its interior have recorded no significant rainfall for many years. The desert lies between the Pacific Ocean to the west and the Andes to the east, forming a narrow north-south strip along the coast.

The Atacama covers roughly 105,000 square kilometres (about 41,000 sq mi), though broader definitions include the surrounding arid lands. Three things cause its dryness. The cold Humboldt Current offshore suppresses evaporation and cloud formation, the subtropical high-pressure system inhibits precipitation, and the Andes block moist air from the Amazon Basin. Most of the region gets only a few millimetres of rain a year, and some central areas can go decades without measurable precipitation.

Some life persists anyway. Vegetation is sparse in the hyper-arid core, but cacti, shrubs, and hardy grasses grow in less extreme zones. Coastal fog, known locally as camanchaca, supplies moisture to some ecosystems. Insects, reptiles, birds, and mammals adapted to aridity live there, and high-altitude wetlands and salt flats support flamingos and other Andean species.

Indigenous peoples have lived in the desert for a long time, including the Atacameño, or Likan Antai, who built settlements in oases and river valleys. The region came under Spanish control during European colonization. In the 19th century it became economically important for its deposits of nitrates, copper, and other minerals. Disputes over these resources helped cause the War of the Pacific (1879 to 1884), after which Chile gained extensive desert territories that Peru and Bolivia had held.

Today the Atacama is a major mining centre, especially for copper and lithium. It is also one of the best places on Earth for astronomy, thanks to its high elevation, minimal cloud cover, low humidity, and little light pollution. The Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and several facilities on Cerro Paranal and La Silla are among the major observatories in or near the region.

Tourists and researchers also visit the desert, which has salt flats, volcanoes, geysers, and eroded rock formations. Its dry, Mars-like conditions have made it a testing ground for space exploration technology and a place to study the limits of life in extreme environments.

Moving to a new city feels, at first, like stepping into the life of someone braver than I am. The decision usually starts out abstract: a job offer, a school, a relationship, a vague hunger to start over. On paper the move looks clean and purposeful. In practice it means cardboard boxes, forwarded mail, a GPS speaking in a robotic voice, and the shock of waking up in a room where the light falls differently across the wall. The pleasures and the costs arrive together, so tangled that I can hardly pull one from the other.

One of the best things about a new city is the chance to see yourself differently. In the place you have always lived, repetition settles your identity. You are someone's child, someone's friend, the person who orders the usual at the coffee shop or avoids certain streets because of old memories. In a new city nobody knows those stories unless you tell them. That anonymity can be lonely, and it can also be a relief. You can become more social or more private, and try new routines and neighborhoods, even a new version of your personality. The city only wants to know how you will move through it now.

Discovery is a pleasure too, and a simple one. Ordinary life turns into exploration, and buying groceries becomes a minor expedition. You notice the architecture, the slang, the way people wait in line or greet strangers. You learn where the best bread is, which park is quietest at dusk, which train platform fills up fastest in the rain. These details pile up slowly, and each one makes the unfamiliar feel a little more like home. Daily life turns out to be unfixed, and it can still surprise you.

But the costs are real, and they are harder to calculate than rent and moving trucks. The most obvious is homesickness, though the word sounds too soft for what it sometimes is. Missing people is only part of it. You also miss the version of yourself that existed effortlessly among them. In your old city, you knew instinctively how to belong. In the new one, belonging is work. You have to build a life almost from scratch: find a doctor, a mechanic, a favorite café, a person to call when something breaks. Even small errands wear you out when you have no familiarity to cushion them.

Then there is the arithmetic of distance. Moving often means accepting that love gets less convenient. Friendships that proximity once sustained have to survive on texts, planned calls, and expensive visits. Family milestones happen without you, or you go back and find that "home" kept changing while you were gone. The city you left does not wait, preserved for your return. It moves on, as you do. There is grief in realizing that.

Perhaps that is part of what moving teaches: a life can only expand by being unsettled. The new city gives you freedom and novelty, and it charges you in uncertainty and loss. Moving means agreeing to that exchange. Over time, if you are lucky, the strange streets become your streets. The costs do not disappear, but they start to look like the price of growing larger than the life you once knew.

# Major hospital network reports data breach affecting thousands of patients

A large regional hospital network said Tuesday that it is investigating a data breach that may have exposed the personal and medical information of thousands of patients.

The network operates several hospitals, outpatient clinics, and specialty care centers across the region. It said it detected suspicious activity in its computer systems earlier this month. Officials said the organization moved quickly to contain the incident, started an internal investigation, and hired outside cybersecurity experts to determine the scope of the breach.

Preliminary findings suggest unauthorized actors may have accessed patient records containing names, dates of birth, addresses, phone numbers, medical record numbers, insurance details, and, in some cases, limited clinical information. Officials said there is currently no evidence that financial account or payment card data was compromised, though the investigation is ongoing.

"We take the privacy and security of our patients' information extremely seriously," the network said in its statement. "Upon discovering this issue, we immediately implemented containment measures, notified law enforcement, and began working with leading forensic specialists to assess what information may have been affected."

The network did not say how many patients are involved but called the breach "significant." Affected patients are expected to be notified by mail in the coming weeks, and the network said it will offer eligible patients free credit monitoring and identity protection services as a precaution.

Hospital operations have continued during the investigation. Some administrative systems were temporarily taken offline, which delayed scheduling and access to certain online services. Officials said emergency departments and inpatient care were not disrupted.

Cybersecurity experts say healthcare organizations are attractive targets because of the volume of sensitive personal and medical data they hold. Unlike a stolen credit card number, which can be canceled, medical records can contain permanent identifying details that may be used for identity theft, insurance fraud, or phishing.

"This type of incident can have long-lasting consequences for patients," said one data privacy analyst who is not affiliated with the network. "Even if clinical care is unaffected, the loss of trust can be substantial, especially when health information is involved."

Regulators are likely to review the breach under federal health privacy rules, including the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, or HIPAA. The law requires covered entities to safeguard patient information and to notify individuals when certain breaches occur.

Patients are advised to watch for unexpected bills, insurance statements, or suspicious emails and phone calls that refer to their medical care. The network said it is strengthening system security and reviewing access controls.

I think a good teacher needs more than a strong grasp of the subject. Knowledge matters, but information alone rarely makes a student curious, confident, or different afterward. What I look for is patience, passion, empathy, and the ability to make students feel seen. The best teachers build a room where learning seems possible.

Patience comes first for me. Students learn at different speeds and think in different ways, and a good teacher knows this. When a student struggles, they try another explanation, another example, or another approach instead of getting frustrated. That tells the student that difficulty is not failure and that understanding sometimes takes a while. For students who doubt themselves, this can make all the difference. A patient teacher ends up teaching perseverance along with the subject.

Passion comes next. Students can tell when a teacher cares about the material, and enthusiasm spreads. Someone who speaks about literature, science, history, or mathematics with real interest can make a hard topic come alive, and a lesson stops being a list of facts and becomes something students remember. Seeing that also teaches them that learning can be a source of joy as well as an obligation.

Empathy matters just as much. A good teacher remembers what it feels like to be confused, nervous, or afraid of getting something wrong. They know students carry things nobody sees, such as trouble at home, stress, insecurity, loneliness, or pressure to succeed, so they treat students with kindness and respect. They listen, and they notice when someone has gone quiet or seems discouraged. Sometimes the most useful thing a teacher can give is encouragement at the right moment, and an explanation can wait. A student who feels understood is more likely to speak up, take risks, and believe they can improve.

Kindness does not mean lowering standards, though. Some of the most effective teachers expect a great deal because they see what their students could do. They push students to think harder, work more carefully, and aim higher than they would alone. What makes this work is that the demands come with support. These teachers ask for excellence and then help students reach it.

The effect of a good teacher also outlasts the classroom. Years later, students may have forgotten the lessons, dates, and formulas, but they often remember how the teacher made them feel. They remember the one who believed in them when they were unsure, who woke an interest they had never considered, or who showed them that their voice counted. Teaching, in that sense, shapes character and possibility as well as education.

So my answer is that a good teacher combines knowledge with humanity. They guide, challenge, encourage, and inspire, and they help students learn about themselves as well as the world. I think that is why such a teacher can matter to someone for a lifetime.

# Commit message style guide

Good commit messages make changes easier to review and decisions easier to understand later. They also make `git log` and `git blame` far more useful when you're debugging. Follow these conventions for every commit.

## Structure

```
<subject line>

<body>

<footer>
```

Separate the subject from the body with a blank line. The body and footer are optional for trivial changes.

## Subject line

- Limit it to 50 characters. The hard limit is 72.
- Use the imperative mood: "Add retry logic," not "Added retry logic" or "Adds retry logic." A good test is that the subject should complete the sentence, "If applied, this commit will…"
- Capitalize the first word.
- Omit the trailing period.
- Be specific. "Fix bug" and "Update code" say nothing. "Fix null check in user lookup" does.

If your team uses prefixes such as `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, or `refactor:` (Conventional Commits), apply them consistently and keep the total length within the limit.

## Body

Use the body to explain what changed and why, not how. The diff already shows how. Consider addressing:

- What problem prompted this change?
- Why did you choose this approach over alternatives?
- What side effects or limitations should reviewers know about?

Wrap lines at 72 characters. Use hyphens or asterisks for bullet points when listing discrete changes.

## Footer

Use the footer for metadata:

- Issue references: `Fixes #123`, `Refs #456`
- Breaking changes: `BREAKING CHANGE: description`
- Co-authors: `Co-authored-by: Name <email>`

## Scope of a commit

Make each commit a single logical change. If you need "and" in your subject line, consider splitting the commit. Avoid mixing formatting changes with functional changes, since that makes review and reverting harder.

## Examples

Weak:

```
fixed stuff
```

Strong:

```
Fix race condition in session cleanup

The cleanup job could delete sessions that were being
refreshed concurrently, logging users out unexpectedly.
Acquire a row-level lock before checking expiration.

Fixes #482
```

## Things to avoid

- Vague messages: "WIP," "misc fixes," "updates"
- Describing the file instead of the change
- Referencing context only you have ("as discussed")
- Blaming or editorializing ("fix stupid bug")
- Committing generated noise without explanation

## Final check

Before committing, ask: *Would someone reading this in two years understand why this change was made?* If not, add more context.

# Tbilisi

Tbilisi (Georgian: თბილისი), historically known as Tiflis, is the capital and largest city of Georgia. It lies on the banks of the Mtkvari (Kura) River. In the early 2020s it had about 1.2 million people, roughly a third of the country's population. It is a major cultural, economic, and transport center in the South Caucasus.

## History

According to tradition, King Vakhtang I Gorgasali of Iberia founded the city in the 5th century AD after finding warm sulfur springs while hunting. The name comes from the Old Georgian *tbili*, meaning "warm." His successors moved the royal seat to Tbilisi, and the city grew in importance despite repeated invasions by Persians, Byzantines, Arabs, Mongols, and Turkic dynasties.

Tbilisi prospered during the Georgian Golden Age under King David IV and Queen Tamar in the 12th and early 13th centuries. It was later sacked several times, notably by Timur and by the Persian ruler Agha Mohammad Khan in 1795. Russia annexed Georgia in the early 19th century, and Tbilisi became the administrative center of the Caucasus Viceroyalty. After a brief independence from 1918 to 1921, it became the capital of the Georgian Soviet Socialist Republic. Georgia regained independence in 1991. Since then Tbilisi has seen political upheaval, including the Rose Revolution of 2003, and considerable modernization.

## Geography and climate

The city sits in a valley surrounded by mountains and hills, at roughly 400 to 770 meters above sea level. Its climate is transitional between humid subtropical and continental, with hot summers and cool winters.

## Culture and architecture

Tbilisi's architecture is eclectic, mixing medieval, neoclassical, Art Nouveau, Soviet, and contemporary styles. The Old Town (Dzveli Tbilisi) has narrow streets, carved wooden balconies, and the sulfur baths of Abanotubani. Landmarks include the Narikala Fortress, the Metekhi Church, the Sioni Cathedral, the Holy Trinity Cathedral (Sameba), and the modern Bridge of Peace. The Kartlis Deda ("Mother of Georgia") statue overlooks the city from Sololaki Ridge.

The city has many theaters, museums, and festivals, among them the Georgian National Museum and the Rustaveli Theatre. Georgian food, including *khachapuri*, *khinkali*, and local wines, is central to the city's identity. Its nightlife and electronic music scene are also known abroad.

## Economy and transport

Tbilisi is the country's financial and commercial center. Its main sectors are services, tourism, trade, and manufacturing. The Tbilisi Metro, opened in 1966, is the main rapid transit system, supplemented by buses, minibuses, and a cable car. Tbilisi International Airport is the country's principal gateway.

## See also

- Georgia (country)
- Kartli
- List of cities in Georgia

# Record Turnout in Tuesday's School Board Election in Maplewood County

**Voters surge to the polls in the district's highest-participation off-year race in decades**

MAPLEWOOD — Residents of Maplewood County turned out in record numbers Tuesday to elect three members to the school board, with election officials reporting that 41 percent of registered voters cast ballots. That is more than double the turnout of the last school board election and the highest for a stand-alone local race in the county's recorded history.

The County Elections Office said 38,214 of the district's 93,200 registered voters participated, compared with roughly 17 percent two years ago. Several precincts reported lines that stretched out the door during the after-work rush, and the polls at Lincoln Elementary stayed open 25 minutes past the scheduled 7 p.m. closing time so those already waiting could vote.

"We prepared for a busy day, but nothing like this," said Dolores Whitfield, the county's elections director. "By noon we had already surpassed the total in-person turnout from the last cycle."

The campaign was contentious, focused on a proposed budget shortfall, school consolidation plans, and debates over curriculum and class sizes. Six candidates competed for three open seats. The race drew unusually large campaign spending for a local contest, along with a series of packed candidate forums.

Parent groups on both sides of the consolidation debate organized door-knocking efforts and carpools to the polls. Student volunteers from Maplewood High School also ran a registration drive in the fall that added nearly 1,800 new voters to the rolls.

"I've lived here 30 years and never voted in a school board race until this year," said Marcus Delgado, 52, a father of two who waited about 20 minutes to vote at Lincoln Elementary. "Decisions about my kids' classrooms are being made, and I wanted a say."

Ruth Ann Kessler, a retired teacher, said the stakes brought her out. "Closing a school affects the whole neighborhood, not just the families who go there," she said.

Preliminary results show incumbent Priya Raman leading the field, followed by newcomers Thomas Berglund and Angela Ortiz, who hold the other two winning positions. The margin between third and fourth place was fewer than 400 votes. The elections office said final results will not be certified until provisional and mail-in ballots are counted next week.

Whitfield said her office would review the day's operations to prepare for future high-turnout elections. "This is a good problem to have," she said. "We hope it's a sign of lasting engagement."

The new board members will be sworn in at the first meeting of the new year.

That is more than double the turnout of the last school board election and the highest for a stand-alone local race in the county's recorded history.

The County Elections Office said 38,214 of the district's 93,200 registered voters participated, compared with roughly 17 percent two years ago. Several precincts reported lines that stretched out the door during the after-work rush, and the polls at Lincoln Elementary stayed open 25 minutes past the scheduled 7 p.m. closing time so those already waiting could vote.

"We prepared for a busy day, but nothing like this," said Dolores Whitfield, the county's elections director. "By noon we had already surpassed the total in-person turnout from the last cycle."

The campaign was contentious, focused on a proposed budget shortfall, school consolidation plans, and debates over curriculum and class sizes. Six candidates competed for three open seats. The race drew unusually large campaign spending for a local contest, along with a series of packed candidate forums.

Parent groups on both sides of the consolidation debate organized door-knocking efforts and carpools to the polls. Student volunteers from Maplewood High School also ran a registration drive in the fall that added nearly 1,800 new voters to the rolls.

"I've lived here 30 years and never voted in a school board race until this year," said Marcus Delgado, 52, a father of two who waited about 20 minutes to vote at Lincoln Elementary. "Decisions about my kids' classrooms are being made, and I wanted a say."

Ruth Ann Kessler, a retired teacher, said the stakes brought her out. "Closing a school affects the whole neighborhood, not just the families who go there," she said.

Preliminary results show incumbent Priya Raman leading the field, followed by newcomers Thomas Berglund and Angela Ortiz, who hold the other two winning positions. The margin between third and fourth place was fewer than 400 votes. The elections office said final results will not be certified until provisional and mail-in ballots are counted next week.

Whitfield said her office would review the day's operations to prepare for future high-turnout elections. "This is a good problem to have," she said. "We hope it's a sign of lasting engagement."

The new board members will be sworn in at the first meeting of the new year.

Voyager 1

Voyager 1 is a robotic space probe operated by NASA. It launched on 5 September 1977 as part of the Voyager program and was designed to study the outer Solar System. After completing its original mission, it kept going outward and is now the most distant human-made object from Earth.

The Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) built Voyager 1, and a Titan IIIE rocket carried it up from Cape Canaveral, Florida. It launched after its twin, Voyager 2, but took a faster trajectory and reached Jupiter and Saturn first. The mission used a rare planetary alignment that let spacecraft visit several outer planets using gravitational assists.

Voyager 1 reached Jupiter in 1979 and returned detailed images of the planet's atmosphere, including its turbulent cloud bands and the Great Red Spot. It found evidence of active volcanism on Io, the first such activity observed beyond Earth. It also gathered new information on Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto, and on Jupiter's magnetosphere and ring system.

In 1980 the probe flew past Saturn and its moon Titan. Titan was a major priority because of its dense atmosphere. Voyager 1 confirmed that the atmosphere is rich in nitrogen, though an opaque haze kept the surface out of view. It also returned extensive observations of Saturn's rings, moons, and magnetic environment. The trajectory needed for the Titan flyby sent the spacecraft out of the plane of the Solar System, which ended any chance of further planetary encounters.

Voyager 1 then began an extended mission to study the outer heliosphere, the region influenced by the solar wind. In August 2012, NASA announced that it had become the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space, crossing the heliopause, where the Sun's influence gives way to the interstellar medium. Its instruments still measure charged particles, magnetic fields, and plasma conditions in this poorly understood region.

The probe also carries the Golden Record, a phonograph record of sounds, images, and messages meant to portray the diversity of life and culture on Earth. It was conceived as a symbolic message to any future finders and remains one of the mission's best-known features.

Voyager 1 is still in contact with Earth through NASA's Deep Space Network, although its power supply declines as its radioisotope thermoelectric generators lose output. NASA has extended the mission repeatedly, and the probe continues to send back scientific data as it travels deeper into interstellar space.

## Pivot tables user guide

A pivot table summarizes large sets of spreadsheet data without manual sorting, filtering, or formulas. You can use it to group information, calculate totals, and spot trends.

### When to use a pivot table
Use a pivot table when you want to:
- Total sales by region, product, or salesperson
- Count records, such as customers or orders
- Compare values across categories
- Rearrange data without changing the original table
- Explore patterns in large datasets

### Before you begin
Make sure your source data:
- Is organized in rows and columns
- Has a single header row
- Contains no completely blank rows or columns
- Uses one data type in each column, such as dates, numbers, or text

Example source columns might include `Date`, `Region`, `Product`, `Salesperson`, `Units`, and `Revenue`.

### Creating a pivot table
1. Select any cell in your data range.
2. Open the **Insert** menu and choose **Pivot Table**.
3. Confirm the data range.
4. Choose where to place the pivot table:
   - New worksheet
   - Existing worksheet
5. Click **Create** or **OK**.

A blank pivot table layout and a field list will appear.

### Understanding the pivot table areas
Most pivot table tools have four layout areas:

- **Rows**: displays categories vertically
- **Columns**: displays categories horizontally
- **Values**: shows calculations such as sum, count, or average
- **Filters**: limits the data shown

### Building a basic pivot table
To summarize total revenue by region:
1. Drag **Region** to **Rows**.
2. Drag **Revenue** to **Values**.

The pivot table will show each region with its total revenue.

To compare revenue by region and product:
1. Keep **Region** in **Rows**.
2. Drag **Product** to **Columns**.
3. Keep **Revenue** in **Values**.

### Changing calculations
A value field can often be summarized in different ways, such as:
- Sum
- Count
- Average
- Minimum
- Maximum

To change a calculation:
1. Click the value field in the pivot table or field settings.
2. Open **Value Field Settings** or **Summarize By**.
3. Choose the calculation you want.

### Filtering and sorting
You can refine results by:
- Applying a report filter, such as showing only one year
- Sorting row labels alphabetically or by value
- Expanding or collapsing grouped items

### Refreshing the pivot table
If the source data changes, refresh the pivot table to update the results:
1. Click anywhere in the pivot table.
2. Select **Refresh** from the pivot table toolbar or context menu.

### Tips
- Use clear column names in your source data
- Format numbers for readability, such as currency or percentages
- If dates do not group correctly, check that they are stored as real dates
- Keep source data unchanged and use the pivot table for analysis

# Pivot tables: a user guide

## What is a pivot table?

A pivot table summarizes large datasets without requiring formulas. It lets you group, count, total, and average your data, then rearrange it in seconds to view it from different angles. Use one when you need answers like "What were total sales by region?" or "How many orders did each rep close per month?"

## Before you begin

Make sure your data is ready:

- Include headers. Every column needs a unique, nonblank title.
- Avoid blank rows or columns, which can cause the table to miss data.
- Keep data consistent. Each column should contain one type of information, such as dates or numbers only.

## Creating a pivot table

1. Click any cell inside your data range.
2. Open the **Insert** menu and choose **Pivot Table**.
3. Confirm the data range shown is correct.
4. Choose a destination: a new sheet (recommended) or an existing location.
5. Click **OK** or **Create**.

An empty pivot table appears, along with a field panel listing your column headers.

## Understanding the four areas

The field panel has four boxes. Drag fields into them to build your report.

- Rows: categories listed down the left side (for example, Product).
- Columns: categories listed across the top (for example, Quarter).
- Values: the numbers being calculated (for example, Sum of Revenue).
- Filters: fields that let you limit the whole table to specific items, such as a single year.

## Example

Suppose your data has columns for Region, Salesperson, Month, and Revenue. To see revenue by region and month:

1. Drag **Region** to Rows.
2. Drag **Month** to Columns.
3. Drag **Revenue** to Values.

The table now shows total revenue for each region-month combination, with grand totals along the edges.

## Changing the calculation

By default, numeric fields are summed. To change this, click the field in the Values box, select **Value Field Settings**, and choose another function, such as Count, Average, Max, or Min. You can also display values as a percentage of the total.

## Refining your report

- Sort: click the dropdown arrow beside a row or column label.
- Filter: use the same arrow to uncheck items you want to hide.
- Group: right-click dates to group them by month, quarter, or year.
- Rearrange: drag fields between areas to see the data differently.

## Keeping data current

Pivot tables don't update automatically when source data changes. Right-click the table and select **Refresh**. If you've added new rows, you may need to update the source range under **Change Data Source**.

## Troubleshooting

- Numbers counted instead of summed: the column likely contains text or blanks. Clean the data and refresh.
- Dates won't group: some entries may be stored as text. Convert them to true dates.

# What the Walls Remember

When I was nine, my grandmother took me to the train station in the town where she grew up. It had been closed for decades, its windows clouded and its ticket counter long since stripped of brass. She pressed her palm flat against the wall of the waiting room as though checking a sleeping animal for breath. "I left for the city from this bench," she said. "Your grandfather proposed on that platform." By any architect's measure the building was nothing special. To her, her whole life had swung on it like a door on a hinge.

I think about that moment whenever someone argues that old buildings are obstacles, expensive to maintain and inconvenient to retrofit, standing where something shinier could go. The argument has a point. Old buildings leak, resist new wiring, and often fail modern codes, and sentiment won't pay for a new roof. I don't believe every old structure deserves rescue. Surviving doesn't make a building sacred.

But some deserve it, and I've come to believe the reasons are practical as well as tender.

For one, an old building holds a kind of memory that no archive can. A photograph shows you how a street looked, but a building lets you stand inside the proportions people once considered normal. You feel how low the ceilings were, how narrow the stairs, how much the light depended on windows rather than switches. History gets concrete when you have to duck through its doorway.

Old buildings also carry craftsmanship we've mostly stopped paying for. The library in my hometown, a century-old building I haunted as a teenager, had tiny acorns carved into the banister. No one required them, and no budget meeting would approve them today. Generations of restless kids ran their hands over those acorns, and I suspect they taught us, without anyone saying so, that ordinary places could be made with care.

Then there's continuity. Neighborhoods built entirely of new construction can feel oddly weightless, like a stage set waiting for a story. Old buildings give a place the sense of having been lived in. They let a newcomer and a lifelong resident share a landmark, even if they remember it differently, and that shared reference point holds a neighborhood together. It is easier to lose than to rebuild.

Last, there's waste. The greenest building, as preservationists like to say, is often the one already standing. Demolition throws away the energy and materials embedded in it and fills landfills besides.

The train station was eventually torn down for a parking lot. Last year I drove through town and tried to find the spot where the bench had been. I couldn't. The asphalt was smooth and the painted lines were crisp, and nothing indicated that a proposal, or a departure, had ever happened there.

That's what I'd want the skeptics to understand. We preserve buildings because they hold the places where our lives took shape, and once they're gone, so are the bench and the wall my grandmother touched, and so is the proof.

The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 between the forces of William, Duke of Normandy, and King Harold Godwinson of England. It was the decisive battle of the Norman Conquest of England and led to Norman rule. The battle is named after the nearby town of Hastings, but it took place about 7 miles (11 km) to the northwest, near the present town of Battle in East Sussex.

The conflict arose from a disputed succession to the English throne. After Edward the Confessor died in January 1066, Harold Godwinson was crowned king. William claimed that Edward had earlier promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn to support his claim. A third claimant, Harald Hardrada of Norway, also invaded England. Harold defeated and killed Hardrada at the Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066, but the victory left his army exhausted.

Meanwhile, William crossed the English Channel and landed at Pevensey on 28 September 1066. He marched into Sussex, built a prefabricated castle at Hastings, and raided the surrounding countryside, partly to draw Harold south. Harold advanced rapidly from London with his household troops, the housecarls, and the levies of the shires, known as the fyrd.

The two armies met on Senlac Hill. Harold's forces formed a dense shield wall along the ridge, while William's army was made up of infantry, archers, and cavalry. The battle lasted most of the day and was hard fought. The English line repelled the first Norman assaults. At one point rumors spread that William had been killed, but he is said to have lifted his helmet to show he was alive and rally his troops.

The turning point came when parts of the English line broke formation, possibly in pursuit of retreating Normans. Historians still debate whether those retreats were genuine or feigned, but they let the Norman cavalry isolate and destroy parts of Harold's army. Late in the day Harold was killed. Tradition says an arrow struck him in the eye, though the exact manner of his death is uncertain. With the king dead and much of the English nobility slain, resistance collapsed.

William was crowned King William I of England on 25 December 1066. The conquest changed English society, aristocracy, language, and government, and tied England more closely to continental Europe. The Bayeux Tapestry, one of the main visual records of the conquest, depicts the battle.

# Transit Strike Halts Buses and Trains, Leaving Thousands of Commuters Stranded

**Union rejects final offer as talks collapse overnight; city braces for second day of disruption**

Hundreds of thousands of commuters scrambled for alternatives Monday after public-transit workers walked off the job at dawn, shutting down bus and rail service across the metropolitan region.

The Metro Transit Workers Union, which represents roughly 8,200 drivers, mechanics, and station staff, began the strike at 4 a.m. after contract negotiations with the Regional Transit Authority broke down late Sunday. It is the first systemwide work stoppage in 14 years.

"We didn't want to be here," said union president Dolores Reyes, speaking from a picket line outside the Eastside bus depot. "But workers who keep this city moving can't be asked to fall behind on rent while costs rise every year."

The union is seeking a 9 percent wage increase over three years, stronger protections against assaults on drivers, and limits on mandatory overtime. Transit officials countered with a 5 percent raise and said they could not meet the remaining demands without raising fares or cutting routes.

"Our offer was fair and fiscally responsible," Authority spokesperson Martin Vail said in a statement. "We remain at the table and urge the union to return to negotiations so riders can get back to their lives."

Highways clogged before sunrise, with traffic officials reporting delays up to 70 percent longer than normal. Ride-share prices surged, and bike-share stations in the downtown core were emptied by 8 a.m. Several major employers encouraged staff to work from home.

At Central Station, normally packed with morning travelers, a handful of people stood reading posted closure notices. Marcus Hill, a hospital cafeteria worker, said he had walked two miles before finding a friend to drive him the rest of the way.

"I support the drivers, I really do," Hill said. "But I can't afford to miss shifts either. I'm stuck in the middle."

Schools reported higher-than-usual absences, and the district said it would keep yellow school buses running, since those are operated by a separate contractor. Paratransit service for riders with disabilities is operating at limited capacity under an emergency agreement, though advocates say wait times have stretched beyond two hours.

Mayor Elaine Cho called on both sides to resume talks immediately and offered city staff as mediators. "Every day this continues costs working families and local businesses," she said.

Economists estimate the shutdown could cost the regional economy $30 million per day in lost productivity and sales.

No new negotiating session has been scheduled. The union said it will continue picketing until it receives a "serious proposal," while the Authority said contingency planning is underway for a prolonged stoppage.

Some old buildings deserve to be preserved because they still matter to the people around them. Age alone is no reason. A cracked wall or a faded sign does not become meaningful just by surviving. But certain buildings hold memory, craftsmanship, and the evidence of how people once imagined their lives, and keeping them lets different generations keep talking to each other.

I think of old buildings as public memory. Families keep photo albums, letters, and heirlooms because objects can hold feeling in ways facts cannot, and cities and towns need the same thing. A preserved train station, schoolhouse, church, or row of apartments tells us more about the people who built a place than a plaque can. The width of a staircase, the hand-carved trim around a doorway, the wear in the stone steps: these details show that history was lived physically. Someone climbed those stairs every day. Someone stood in that hallway waiting for news, or for work, or for grief to pass. When such buildings go, part of our shared memory goes with them.

Old buildings also offer a kind of beauty that is hard to reproduce. Many were built with patience and durable materials, with ornament that reflected pride rather than efficiency. Even modest ones show a human touch: uneven bricks laid by hand, wooden floors polished by decades of footsteps, windows placed for grace as well as function. So much construction today is driven by speed and profit, and these buildings show that usefulness and beauty don't have to compete. They make me pay attention to texture and detail.

There is an ethical reason too. Demolishing and rebuilding is not always progress, and sometimes it amounts to forgetting under another name. Of course, not every old building can or should be saved. Cities have to change, and communities need housing, safety, and accessibility. But when a building has real architectural distinction or deep cultural importance, preserving it shows respect. It says the people who came before us are not disposable, and that the struggles and achievements that shaped a neighborhood still have meaning. That goes especially for places tied to ordinary people rather than the wealthy or famous. A factory, a corner store, or a union hall may tell a more democratic story than a mansion ever could.

What moves me most is how preserved buildings make time feel layered instead of lost. Walking into an old library or courthouse, you feel, even briefly, that your own life is part of a longer human story. The building has outlasted fashions, governments, and private worries, and it still stands, asking for care rather than pity. At its best, preservation is humble. It admits that we are not the first people to love a place, and that whoever comes after us will need something solid to remember it by.

# Contributing to the docs

This guide covers how to contribute to the documentation, whether you're fixing a typo or writing a new tutorial.

## Ways to contribute

- Fix errors: typos, broken links, outdated screenshots, or incorrect code samples.
- Improve clarity: rewrite confusing explanations or add missing context.
- Write new content: tutorials, how-to guides, and reference pages.
- Review pull requests: feedback from someone new to the pages catches things regular contributors miss.
- Report issues: if you spot a problem but can't fix it, open an issue.

## Getting set up

1. Fork the repository and clone your fork locally.
2. Install dependencies with `npm install`.
3. Start the local preview server with `npm run dev`.
4. Open `http://localhost:3000`. Your changes update live.

For small edits, you can also click "Edit this page" at the bottom of any page to make changes directly on GitHub.

## Making a change

1. Create a branch with a descriptive name, such as `fix-install-typo` or `add-auth-guide`.
2. Make your edits in the `docs/` directory. Files are written in Markdown.
3. Run `npm run lint` to check formatting and `npm run build` to confirm the site builds without broken links.
4. Commit with a clear message, such as `Fix incorrect flag in CLI reference`.
5. Push your branch and open a pull request.

## Style guidelines

Please follow these conventions so the docs read consistently:

- Use plain language. Prefer short sentences and avoid unnecessary jargon.
- Address the reader as "you."
- Use active voice. Write "Run the command," not "The command should be run."
- Put code in code blocks and specify the language for syntax highlighting.
- Use sentence case for headings.
- Test every snippet before submitting it, so examples run as written.
- Write descriptive link text. Avoid "click here."

## Structure of the docs

We organize content into four types:

- Tutorials: step-by-step lessons for beginners.
- How-to guides: solutions to specific problems.
- Reference: precise technical descriptions.
- Explanations: background and concepts.

Try to keep each page focused on one type.

## Pull request checklist

Before submitting, confirm that:

- [ ] The site builds locally without errors.
- [ ] Links and code samples work.
- [ ] Your changes follow the style guidelines.
- [ ] The PR description explains what changed and why.

## Review process

A maintainer will typically respond within a few days. We may suggest edits, which is a normal part of review. Once approved, your changes will be merged and published automatically.

## Community expectations

Be kind and patient with other contributors. Everyone must follow our Code of Conduct.

## Need help?

Ask questions in our discussion forum or comment on an issue. We're happy to help first-time contributors get started.

The **Hanseatic League** was a commercial and defensive confederation of merchant guilds and market towns in northwestern and central Europe. It dominated maritime trade in the Baltic and North Seas from the late 12th to the 17th century. At its height it linked nearly 200 towns, from London and Bruges to Novgorod and Bergen, and it shaped the economies and towns of medieval northern Europe.

The League grew out of the expansion of German merchants, especially from cities such as Lübeck and Hamburg, who wanted protection and privileges while trading abroad. Lübeck, founded in 1143 and located between the North and Baltic Seas, became the League's leading city. By the 13th century, merchant communities from German-speaking towns had set up trading outposts, known as *Kontore*, in London, Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod. These were warehouses, offices, and legal communities that protected Hanseatic interests.

The League was not a state. It had no formal constitution, permanent army, or centralized administration, and functioned as a loose association of towns and merchants with shared economic interests. Decisions were made at assemblies called the *Hansetag*, where representatives of member cities negotiated commercial policy, mutual defense, and relations with foreign rulers. Membership was fluid, and cities took part to different degrees.

Its economic power rested on the exchange of regional goods. Grain, timber, wax, fur, and fish came from the east; cloth, wine, salt, and metal goods came from the west and south. Hanseatic merchants built efficient shipping networks and standardized commercial practices, which lowered transaction costs and increased trust over long distances. When necessary, the League used embargoes and naval force to defend its privileges, as in its conflicts with Denmark in the 14th century.

From the late 15th century the League declined gradually. Stronger territorial states, trade routes shifting toward the Atlantic, growing Dutch and English competition, and internal divisions all weakened it. Its overseas privileges were progressively reduced and several *Kontore* closed. Some cities still identified with the League, but its political significance had largely disappeared by the 17th century. The last *Hansetag* met in 1669.

The League influenced the urban culture, architecture, and commercial law of northern Europe. Former Hanseatic cities such as Lübeck, Hamburg, Bremen, and Tallinn still have brick Gothic buildings and civic traditions that date from the League. Historians often regard it as an early example of transnational commercial cooperation and urban networking in Europe.

# Bike-share FAQ

## Getting started

**How do I rent a bike?**
Download our app and create an account. Then find a nearby station, tap "Unlock," and scan the QR code on the bike. You can also unlock bikes at station kiosks using a credit card.

**How much does it cost?**
- Single ride: $1 to unlock, plus $0.15 per minute
- Day pass: $12, with unlimited 30-minute rides for 24 hours
- Monthly membership: $20, with unlimited 45-minute rides
- Annual membership: $150, with unlimited 45-minute rides

Discounted memberships are available for students, seniors, and low-income residents. Visit our website to apply.

## Using the service

**How long can I keep a bike?**
Ride as long as you like, but time beyond your plan's included minutes is billed at $0.15 per minute. For longer trips, dock the bike and check out another to reset your time.

**Where can I return my bike?**
Return it to any station with an open dock. Push the front wheel firmly into the dock until the light turns green. If a station is full, use the app to find the nearest one with space, and you'll receive a free 10-minute extension.

**Do I need to bring a helmet?**
Helmets aren't provided, but we strongly recommend wearing one. Riders under 16 are required by law to wear a helmet.

**Are electric bikes available?**
Yes. E-bikes are marked with a green stripe and cost an additional $0.10 per minute. They assist you up to 20 mph.

## Safety and problems

**What if a bike is damaged?**
Check the brakes, tires, and seat before riding. If something seems wrong, press the red "Report" button on the bike's screen or use the app. Then return it to a dock to take it out of service. You won't be charged for rides under one minute.

**What if the bike is lost or stolen?**
Lock the bike with the built-in cable lock whenever you pause. Use the "Hold" feature in the app for short stops. If a bike is lost or stolen while in your care, report it within 24 hours. Unreported losses may result in a $250 fee.

**Can I ride at night?**
Yes. Our bikes have built-in front and rear lights that activate automatically.

## Account help

**Can I share my membership?**
No. Memberships are personal, and each account can only unlock one bike at a time. Group rides require multiple accounts.

**How do I cancel my membership?**
Go to Settings > Membership in the app and select "Cancel." Monthly plans end at the close of the billing period, and annual plans can be refunded within 14 days.

**Who do I contact for help?**
Call 555-0142, email help@citybikeshare.example, or use the in-app chat. Support is available daily from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.

## Plugin system

The editor has a plugin system for extending it without modifying the main application. Plugins can add commands, sidebar panels, language support, formatters, themes, and event-driven behavior.

### Plugin structure

Each plugin lives in its own directory and must include a manifest file named `plugin.json`. A typical plugin looks like this:

```text
my-plugin/
  plugin.json
  main.js
  README.md
  assets/
```

The `plugin.json` file defines metadata and the plugin entry point:

```json
{
  "id": "example.hello-world",
  "name": "Hello World",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "main.js",
  "enabled": true
}
```

Required fields:

- `id`: Unique plugin identifier.
- `name`: Human-readable name.
- `version`: Plugin version.
- `main`: Entry script loaded by the editor.

Optional fields include `description`, `author`, and `dependencies`.

### Lifecycle

When the editor starts, it scans the plugin directory, reads each manifest, and loads enabled plugins. The entry script must export an `activate` function. If a `deactivate` function is present, the editor calls it when the plugin is unloaded or the editor exits.

Example:

```js
export function activate(api) {
  api.commands.register("hello.sayHello", () => {
    api.window.showMessage("Hello from plugin!");
  });
}

export function deactivate() {
  // Clean up resources here
}
```

Use `activate` to register commands, subscribe to events, or initialize UI elements. Use `deactivate` to dispose of timers, listeners, and temporary state.

### Editor API

Plugins interact with the editor through the `api` object passed to `activate`. Common namespaces include:

- `api.commands`: Register and execute commands.
- `api.window`: Show notifications, dialogs, and UI panels.
- `api.workspace`: Access open files, project folders, and settings.
- `api.editor`: Read or modify the active document.
- `api.events`: Subscribe to editor events such as file open, save, or cursor movement.

Example command registration:

```js
export function activate(api) {
  api.commands.register("example.insertDate", () => {
    const editor = api.editor.getActiveEditor();
    if (!editor) return;

    editor.insertText(new Date().toLocaleDateString());
  });
}
```

### Installation and management

You can install a plugin by copying its directory into the editor's `plugins/` folder or through the built-in plugin manager. The settings interface lets you enable, disable, update, or remove plugins.

If a plugin fails to load, the editor logs the error and continues starting up. Load errors, activation failures, and dependency issues are reported in the developer console.

### Best practices

- Keep each plugin focused on a single responsibility.
- Use stable, namespaced command IDs such as `author.feature.action`.
- Validate settings, and handle missing editor state without crashing.
- Dispose of event listeners during deactivation.
- Avoid blocking operations during activation so startup stays fast.

# The gift of nothing to do

Last summer my phone died on a train, and I had four hours of countryside ahead of me with nothing to look at but the window. For the first twenty minutes I was almost frantic. My hand kept drifting to my pocket like a tongue to a missing tooth. I counted fence posts. I reread the safety instructions above the door. I was, in the plainest sense, bored.

Somewhere past a river I couldn't name, my mind stopped scrambling for input and started producing its own. I remembered a conversation with my grandmother that I hadn't thought about in years. I figured out how to restructure a project at work that had been nagging me for weeks. I invented, for no reason, an elaborate backstory for the man asleep across the aisle. By the time we pulled into the station, I felt strangely rested, as though I'd been somewhere.

I think about that trip often. Boredom used to be unavoidable. It lived in waiting rooms, in long car rides, in the dead hour between homework and dinner. Now I can get rid of it entirely, because every gap in the day can be filled with a feed, a podcast, a scroll. I've become so efficient at escaping boredom that I've almost forgotten what it was for.

I've come to believe it's a kind of internal housekeeping. When nothing is demanding our attention, the mind turns inward and starts sorting. It connects things that don't obviously connect. It surfaces worries we've been outrunning and desires we haven't admitted. Psychologists have linked this idle wandering to creativity and planning, and that matches my experience. My best ideas have never arrived while I was consuming something. They've come in the shower, on walks, and while washing dishes.

Boredom also shows me what I actually want to do, as opposed to what I'm being offered. As a kid, summer boredom eventually pushed me to build a fort, start a terrible comic, or take apart a broken radio. Nobody handed me those projects. They came out of the discomfort of an empty afternoon, and they felt like mine in a way that entertainment never does.

Boredom is unpleasant, and that's the point. It's a signal, like hunger, that something in us wants engagement. The mistake is answering it with whatever is nearest. Fast food quiets hunger without nourishing you, and a scroll quiets boredom without giving the mind anything to chew on.

So I've started a small practice. I leave my phone in my bag while waiting in line. I take walks without headphones. Sometimes I sit on the porch and watch the light change on the neighbor's maple. The first few minutes are always itchy. Then the restlessness gives way to something spacious, and thoughts I didn't know I was carrying begin to surface.

I used to think an empty moment was a wasted one. Now I suspect it's closer to fallow ground, which looks like nothing is happening while the next thing gets ready to grow.

**The Weight of a Hamburger**

When I was nine, I watched my uncle slaughter a pig. I had been told to stay in the truck, and of course I didn't. What I remember is the quiet afterward, how ordinary the men became once it was done, rinsing their hands and talking about the weather. That night we ate pork shoulder. It was delicious, and I could not stop thinking about the pig's eyes.

I've been circling that evening for most of my adult life.

For years I avoided the question the way you avoid a bill you suspect you can't pay. I ate chicken breasts that came in plastic, shaped like nothing that had ever lived. Then I read a book about industrial farming, one of those books whose purpose is to ruin your appetite, and it worked. I became a vegetarian for three years. I was sincere and a little insufferable about it.

What I believed then, and still believe, is that suffering matters. Pigs are intelligent and social, and they feel fear. If I accept that a dog's pain counts for something, I have to explain why a pig's doesn't, and "because it tastes good" is a poor argument. Most of the meat in the world comes from animals that lived in conditions I would call cruel if I saw them applied to anything I loved. That is hard to argue around, and I've stopped trying.

But the certainty I felt as a vegetarian has worn down as life got more complicated, even though the arguments haven't weakened. I spent a winter with relatives whose diet was largely what they raised and hunted, and their relationship to meat was nothing like mine. They knew the animals, thanked them without embarrassment, and wasted nothing. I couldn't honestly say they were doing something worse than I was, standing in a grocery aisle buying almond milk shipped from a drought-stricken valley. Every way of eating costs something, and what differs is how visible the cost is.

That, I think, is where I've landed, uncomfortably. What bothers me most about modern meat is that the killing has been hidden from us. Distance makes cruelty easy. If I'm going to eat an animal, I should be willing to know where it lived and how it was killed. If I can't stand to know, that's information too.

So now I eat meat rarely and try to know its source. I buy from a farmer whose fields I've walked through. Sometimes I fail, and I eat the convenient thing at an airport or a wedding and feel the old pang. I don't think this makes me virtuous. At most it makes me a more thoughtful participant in something I can't fully justify.

I used to want a clean answer, either a rule I could follow or a principle that would let me stop thinking. I've come to distrust that wish. Some questions stay open and keep nagging at you.

I still think about the pig sometimes, and the memory seems to ask me to stay awake while I eat.

# Svalbard Global Seed Vault

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault is a seed storage facility on Spitsbergen, in Norway's Svalbard archipelago, about 1,300 kilometres from the North Pole. It opened in 2008 to hold duplicate samples of seeds from gene banks around the world. If a collection is lost to war, natural disaster, equipment failure, climate change, or poor management, the vault holds a copy.

The vault is built into the side of Platåberget, a sandstone mountain near the settlement of Longyearbyen. The site was chosen for political and environmental reasons. Svalbard is geologically stable, and the cold climate and surrounding permafrost keep the seeds frozen even if the power fails. The seeds are stored at about −18 °C (0 °F), a standard temperature for long-term storage in seed banks.

The vault is sometimes called the "doomsday vault." It is a backup repository, not a conventional seed bank. It does not own the seeds deposited there. Under a "black box" arrangement they remain the property of the depositing institutions, and only the depositor can access its own collection. National, regional, and international gene banks use it as an extra layer of security.

The Government of Norway developed the vault in partnership with the Nordic Genetic Resource Center (NordGen) and the Crop Trust. It can hold millions of seed samples, including food crops and their wild relatives. The collections include wheat, rice, maize, barley, beans, and many other crop species. Plant breeders can draw on this genetic diversity in the future to improve crops and adapt them to changing conditions.

In 2015, the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) became the first institution to withdraw seeds from the vault. Conflict in Syria had disrupted operations at its regional gene bank. ICARDA used the withdrawn seeds to regenerate its collections and later redeposited fresh samples.

The Weight of Paper

After my grandmother died, I found her letters in a shoebox, rubber-banded by year. Mine were in there too, dutiful childhood notes about school and a lost tooth, which she had kept for decades. But it was her side of the correspondence I couldn't stop reading, the letters my mother had saved and passed back to me.

Nothing happens in them. The tomatoes are coming in late. Mrs. Dolan's hip is no better. It rained Tuesday, then Wednesday, then, she wrote, "it seemed to lose interest." I laughed out loud at that, alone in my kitchen, hearing her dry voice come through the slanted blue ink. She had crossed out a word and written another above it, and I could see her hesitate and decide. That small correction told me more about her than any photograph.

I think what we lose when we stop writing letters is the evidence that someone paid attention. A letter is proof that someone sat down and held you in mind for twenty uninterrupted minutes, not while waiting for coffee or half-watching television. Now I send dozens of messages a day. They are quick and warm, but weightless: they arrive mid-distraction and get answered mid-distraction, and almost none are kept, because there are far too many to keep.

Letters also required a patience that shaped what people said. You couldn't fire off a feeling and retract it ten seconds later. You had to let a thought finish itself, and sometimes in the finishing it changed. My grandfather, I learned from the shoebox, once wrote three pages to my grandmother about a quarrel, and the last paragraph contradicts the first. He hadn't meant to forgive her when he began. The letter got him there. A text would have kept him angry, or ended the argument in a single clipped word.

And then there was the waiting. We treat waiting as pure cost now, a flaw to be engineered away. But the days between sending and receiving gave longing somewhere to live. You walked to the mailbox with a small, private hope. When something came, it had traveled to reach you. It had a smudge on it and a faint smell of someone else's house.

Last winter I wrote a letter to an old friend who had moved across the country. It took me an hour and a half, far longer than I expected, because I kept discovering things I hadn't realized I wanted to say. My handwriting had gone ragged from disuse. I crossed out a word and wrote another above it. When I dropped the envelope in the box, I felt oddly exposed, as though I'd handed over something I couldn't edit.

She wrote back three weeks later. I have it still, on my desk, the paper slightly creased where her hand pressed down. It says, among other things, that it has been raining, and that the rain seems to have lost interest.

# Design proposal: caching layer for the web API

## Overview
This document proposes a caching layer for the web API to reduce response latency, lower backend load, and improve scalability. The cache will store frequently requested API responses and serve them without repeated database or downstream service calls.

## Goals
- Reduce average API response time
- Lower database and service load
- Improve throughput during traffic spikes
- Maintain acceptable data freshness
- Provide observability into cache behavior

## Non-goals
- Replacing the primary database
- Caching highly sensitive or user-specific data without additional controls
- Guaranteeing perfectly fresh data for all endpoints

## Architecture
The caching layer will sit between the API application and the backend data sources. The API first checks the cache for a stored response. If a valid entry exists, the API returns it immediately. Otherwise, it fetches the data from the source, returns the response, and writes it to the cache.

We recommend a distributed in-memory store such as Redis for its low latency, support for expiration, and operational maturity. For static or public GET endpoints, a CDN or edge cache may be added later.

## Cache strategy
The initial implementation will use cache-aside:
1. Client requests a resource
2. API looks up the cache key
3. On a hit, return the cached response
4. On a miss, fetch from the backend
5. Store the result in the cache with a TTL
6. Return the response

Cache-aside is simple and fits read-heavy workloads.

## Key design
Cache keys should be deterministic and include:
- Endpoint path
- Normalized query parameters
- API version
- Relevant request context such as locale

Example:
`v1:products:list:category=books:page=2:locale=en-US`

## Expiration and invalidation
Each cached item will have a TTL based on how often its endpoint's data changes:
- Reference data: 1 to 24 hours
- Frequently updated entities: 1 to 5 minutes
- Aggregated results: 30 to 120 seconds

Writes that affect cached resources should invalidate them. For example, when a product is updated, the related product detail and listing keys should be deleted or versioned. Where exact invalidation is difficult, use shorter TTLs.

## Reliability considerations
To avoid cache stampedes, the system should support request coalescing or a soft TTL with background refresh. Negative caching may be used briefly for known missing resources to reduce repeated misses. If the cache is unavailable, the API must fall back to the backend.

## Security
Sensitive data should not be cached unless it is encrypted and scoped per user. Public and shared caches must exclude authenticated or personalized responses by default.

## Observability
Metrics should include:
- Cache hit rate
- Miss rate
- Eviction rate
- Latency by endpoint
- Backend request reduction

We should also add structured logs and dashboards to monitor how well the cache is working.

## Rollout plan
Start with a small set of high-read, low-volatility GET endpoints. Measure hit rate and latency improvements, then expand gradually.

# Library of Alexandria

The Library of Alexandria was one of the most famous libraries of the ancient world and a major center of scholarship in Alexandria, Egypt, during the Hellenistic period. It was tied to the Mouseion ("Temple of the Muses"), a research institution established under the Ptolemaic dynasty after the conquests of Alexander the Great. Many details remain uncertain, but the library has become a symbol of learning and of cultural loss.

The library was probably founded in the early 3rd century BCE, most likely during the reign of Ptolemy I Soter or his son Ptolemy II Philadelphus. The Ptolemies wanted Alexandria to be the leading center of Greek culture and scholarship, so they gathered texts from across the Mediterranean world, including works of literature, philosophy, science, mathematics, and history. According to ancient sources, books arriving in the city were copied, and in some cases the library kept the originals and returned copies to their owners.

The library was part of a wider scholarly community. Resident scholars studied, edited, and compared texts, and they helped establish critical editions of major Greek authors such as Homer. The institution drew Euclid, Eratosthenes, Aristarchus of Samothrace, and Callimachus. Callimachus is traditionally credited with compiling the Pinakes, a vast bibliographic catalogue often regarded as one of the earliest library catalogues in history.

Estimates of the library's size vary widely. Ancient and modern figures range from tens of thousands to several hundred thousand scrolls. Scholars still debate how the library was organized and how the main library related to a possible "daughter library" in the Serapeum.

The destruction of the library is one of the best-known episodes in cultural history, though it likely did not happen in a single catastrophic event. Ancient and later sources connect its decline to several episodes: Julius Caesar's campaign in Alexandria in 48 BCE, political turmoil in the Roman period, and the destruction of pagan institutions in late antiquity, especially during the 4th century CE. Modern historians generally conclude that the library declined gradually over centuries rather than being destroyed all at once.

Since antiquity the library has come to stand for the ideal of universal knowledge and for the fragility of cultural memory. The Bibliotheca Alexandrina in modern Alexandria, inaugurated in 2002, was conceived as a tribute to the ancient institution.

# Hanseatic League

The **Hanseatic League** (also known as the **Hansa**) was a commercial and defensive confederation of merchant guilds and market towns in Northern and Central Europe. It originated in the 12th century and was at its height between the 13th and 15th centuries, when it dominated trade across the Baltic Sea and North Sea regions. Its member cities lay mainly along the coasts of present-day Germany, Poland, the Baltic states, and neighboring regions.

## Origins

The League grew out of associations of German merchants who traveled together for protection against piracy and banditry. Lübeck, founded in 1143, became the gateway to the Baltic, and its rise drove this development. Its 1241 agreement with Hamburg is often cited as an early milestone. Over time, many other towns joined, including Cologne, Bremen, Danzig (Gdańsk), Riga, and Tallinn (Reval).

## Organization

The Hansa was never a state in the modern sense. It had no standing army, permanent treasury, or formal constitution. It was a loose association governed by periodic assemblies called the *Hansetag*, which met mainly in Lübeck. Decisions were enforced through collective economic pressure, such as trade embargoes, and occasionally through military action. Lübeck is generally regarded as the League's leading city, often called its "Queen."

## Trade

Hanseatic merchants traded in bulk commodities. From the east they carried timber, furs, wax, amber, grain, and rye; from the west and south they brought cloth, wine, and manufactured goods. Salted herring from Scania and salt from Lüneburg were also major goods. The League had overseas trading posts, known as *Kontore*, in London (the Steelyard), Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod (the Peterhof). These enclaves had special privileges and operated under their own rules.

## Conflicts

The Hansa's power brought it into conflict with rulers who resented its trading privileges. The largest conflict was a war with Denmark, which ended with the Treaty of Stralsund in 1370 and confirmed Hanseatic dominance in the Baltic. Later, competition from Dutch, English, and Scandinavian merchants steadily eroded its position.

## Decline

From the late 15th century, the League weakened. Strong territorial states rose, trade routes shifted toward the Atlantic, Dutch commercial power grew, and the members were divided among themselves. The loss of privileges, such as the closure of the Steelyard in London in 1598, reduced its influence further. The last formal assembly took place in 1669, though Lübeck, Hamburg, and Bremen kept the Hanseatic name for centuries.

## Legacy

The League left brick Gothic buildings across the Baltic. Hamburg and Bremen still use "Free and Hanseatic City" in their official titles. A modern "New Hanse" and the annual Hanseatic Days commemorate the League.

The Dust Bowl was a period of severe dust storms on the Great Plains of the United States during the 1930s, worst from 1934 to 1936. Prolonged drought, high winds, and farming practices that left the soil open to erosion all played a part. Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico suffered most.

Deep-rooted native grasses had once held the Plains soil in place. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, farmers plowed large areas of prairie for wheat and cattle grazing. High crop prices and the belief that "rain follows the plow" pushed many of them onto marginal land. When drought struck in the early 1930s, the exposed topsoil dried out and strong winds lifted it easily.

The dust storms, sometimes called "black blizzards," carried enormous clouds of soil across towns, farms, and even distant cities. The best known came on April 14, 1935, remembered as Black Sunday, when a wall of dust swept across the southern Plains. The storms destroyed crops, buried machinery, and killed livestock. They also caused a respiratory illness known as "dust pneumonia."

The Dust Bowl made the Great Depression harder to bear. Farm incomes collapsed, banks failed, and many families lost their land. Hundreds of thousands of people left the Plains, especially from Oklahoma and Arkansas, for California and other western states, hoping to find work. They were often called "Okies," although many came from other states. John Steinbeck's *The Grapes of Wrath* later portrayed their experiences.

The federal government responded with conservation and relief measures under President Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal. In 1935 it established the Soil Conservation Service, which promoted contour plowing, crop rotation, strip farming, and shelterbelts of trees to reduce erosion. Assistance programs helped struggling farm families either relocate or stay on their land.

Rainfall gradually returned in the late 1930s, easing the worst conditions. The Dust Bowl is still cited as an example of what unsustainable land use can do.

# The friendship that lives in my pocket

When I was twelve, my best friend moved across the country, and we wrote letters. They were clumsy, full of crossed-out words and drawings in the margins. A reply took two weeks, sometimes three. I remember the small thrill of seeing her handwriting in the mailbox, and how I read each letter so many times that the folds went soft. We lost touch within a year. Back then, distance simply did that.

My own kids will never know that kind of loss, and I'm still deciding how I feel about it.

Social media has rearranged friendship in ways I notice most when I try to explain them. I know what my college roommate had for dinner last night. I know her daughter lost a tooth, that her mother has been ill, that she's frustrated with her job. I haven't spoken to her in four years. Is she my friend? By the old definition, probably not. By the new one, she's someone I "keep up with," which is its own strange category: I feel close to her without any contact at all.

There are real gifts in this. I've watched friendships survive moves, career changes, and the ordinary drift that once ended them. A friend in another time zone sends me voice memos while she walks her dog, and I answer while I do dishes. It's not the same as sitting across from her, but it keeps a thread between us that we can pull tight again. When we finally see each other, we don't start from zero.

The costs are quieter, and I've felt them more as I've gotten older. Social media makes friendship feel like a performance with an audience. I've caught myself composing a moment while I'm still inside it, angling the dinner table for a photo, thinking of a caption while a friend is mid-sentence. The experience becomes content, and the friend turns into a co-star.

It has also made affection cheap. A like costs nothing. A birthday message from a platform's reminder takes four seconds. We send these little tokens and feel we've done the work of caring, but real friendship has always required something less efficient: showing up, sitting in awkward silence, driving across town when someone's life falls apart. No app has automated that, though apps make it easy to feel we don't need to.

Last winter, a friend I'd only ever "liked" from afar posted something vague and sad, a small flare I almost took for scenery. I nearly scrolled past. Instead, I called her. We talked for two hours, and she cried, and I realized how long it had been since I'd heard her actual voice.

Social media widened the net and thinned the rope. What we do with the slack is up to us, and the feed can be the friendship itself or a doorway into one.

I still have my friend's old letters, soft at the folds. I don't want to go back to waiting three weeks for a reply. But I'd like to write like that again: slowly, with crossed-out words, meaning every one.

By Thursday afternoon I often notice a strange shift in the office. People are still answering emails and sitting in meetings, but the energy has changed. Monday's sharpness is gone. Conversations drift, and small tasks take longer than they should. By Friday it sometimes feels like everyone is performing work more than doing it. That feeling has made me increasingly sympathetic to the case for a four-day work week.

The fantasy of one more day to sleep in is certainly appealing, but what persuades me more is the recognition that more time at work doesn't always mean better work. In many office jobs, productivity isn't a simple matter of hours logged. Attention is finite, creativity fades when it is overused, and tired people make sloppier decisions. We often talk as if endurance were the highest professional virtue, but clarity matters more than duration. People aren't machines, and pretending they are usually leads to mediocre work.

I also like that a four-day week treats rest as valuable rather than indulgent. In many work cultures exhaustion is worn as a badge of honor: to be overwhelmed is to be important, to be unavailable is to be needed. That logic feels increasingly hollow to me. Rest is one of the conditions that make responsibility possible. An extra day can mean time to recover, to look after children or parents, to book a doctor's appointment without stress, or to exercise and read. When people have room to live fuller lives, they often return to work more focused and less resentful.

There is also, I think, a moral argument. For generations, technological advances have been sold as a route to efficiency and freedom. For many workers, though, the efficiencies brought higher expectations instead of more leisure. We can answer messages instantly, produce documents faster, and automate routine tasks, and the reward is often more work. A four-day week offers a chance for the benefits of innovation to be shared as time.

Not every profession can adopt the same schedule in the same way. Hospitals, schools, factories, and service industries all have practical constraints. A four-day week won't fix every workplace problem. It needs careful implementation, staffing adjustments, and an honest commitment not to cram five days of meetings into four. But those challenges call for rethinking old assumptions.

To me, the case for a four-day week is a case for dignity. It asks whether work should consume the best of our lives or support them. I think people want to contribute sustainably, with enough of themselves left over for the rest of life.
