# Wildfire forces thousands to evacuate near Cedar Ridge National Park

CEDAR FALLS, Mont. A fast-moving wildfire tore through dry timber along the western edge of Cedar Ridge National Park on Tuesday, forcing the evacuation of more than 3,000 residents and prompting officials to close the park to all visitors.

The blaze, named the Hollow Creek Fire, was first reported shortly after 2 p.m. Monday and has since burned an estimated 14,000 acres. Fire officials said it was zero percent contained as of Wednesday morning.

"This fire is moving faster than anything we've seen in this area in a decade," said Incident Commander Dana Whitfield at an evening briefing. "Dry fuels, low humidity, and gusting winds are all working against us."

Mandatory evacuation orders were issued for the communities of Pine Hollow, Larkspur, and parts of Cedar Falls. An additional 2,000 residents in neighboring areas were told to be ready to leave on short notice. Sheriff's deputies went door to door overnight, and emergency alerts were sent to cell phones throughout the county.

An evacuation center opened at Cedar Falls High School, where the Red Cross provided cots, meals, and information. By midday, more than 400 people had checked in. Many arrived with pets, medications, and little else.

"We had about fifteen minutes to grab what we could," said Maria Delgado, a Larkspur resident who left with her two children and their dog. "I took photo albums, documents, and clothes. You just hope the house is still there when you get back."

Park Superintendent Tom Ellery said all campgrounds and trails had been cleared and that rangers had accounted for all registered backcountry visitors. "Visitor safety is our top priority," he said. "We are also working closely with firefighters to protect historic structures, including the Ridgeline Lodge, which dates to 1932."

More than 600 firefighters, supported by helicopters and air tankers, are battling the flames. Crews have focused on building containment lines near homes and protecting power infrastructure. Two firefighters suffered minor heat-related injuries, officials said. No civilian injuries or deaths have been reported.

Smoke has drifted across the region, and health officials issued air quality warnings for three counties, urging children, older adults, and people with respiratory conditions to stay indoors.

Meteorologists said a slight chance of rain may arrive late Friday, though thunderstorms could also bring dangerous lightning and erratic winds.

Governor Elaine Parks declared a state of emergency Tuesday, freeing up additional state resources. Officials have not determined the cause of the fire, and an investigation is underway.

Residents can find updates and shelter information on the county emergency management website.

# The Weight of Boxes

The first thing I noticed about my new city was the silence, which seemed loud. In my old apartment I knew every sound: the radiator's knock, the upstairs neighbor's heavy footsteps, the bus that groaned past at 6:40 each morning. Here, in a sublet that smelled faintly of someone else's cooking, I lay awake listening to noises I couldn't name.

Moving, it turns out, means losing your fluency. I had lived in my old city for nine years and could get around it half asleep. I knew which grocery store had good tomatoes, which streets flooded in spring, which barista would start my order when I walked in. In the new city I got lost on the way to the pharmacy, and I stood in the cereal aisle for ten minutes, defeated by brands I didn't recognize. It was humbling and a little absurd to feel like a child at thirty-four.

The humbling had an upside. Within a week my attention sharpened in a way it hadn't in years. I noticed the brick on my street, a warm rust that glowed at dusk, and that people here nodded at strangers. I took the long way everywhere because I had no short way yet. A city you don't know makes you look at it, and I had stopped looking at things somewhere along the way. Routine had been wearing my days down until they all felt the same.

Small pleasures followed. A bakery owner started saving me the end pieces of the rye loaf. On Sunday mornings, on a river path, runners and old men with fishing rods shared the same few feet of asphalt in peaceful disregard. No one had told me about either place. I found them by wandering.

The costs were real too. On a Tuesday something funny happened and I reached for my phone to tell a friend, then worked out the time zones and put it down. In the second month, when the novelty thinned, I understood that friendship can't be unpacked like a box. It builds slowly, through repetition and accident, through being around. I had traded people who knew my history for people who knew only my present, and that was lonelier than I'd expected.

I've been here a year now. The bus no longer sounds foreign. I have a tomato place. Last month a woman at the bakery asked how my week was going, and I realized I had a week worth describing. I still miss the old city, the way you miss a language you used to speak well.

I think homesickness is the price of having loved a place, and I don't regret paying it. Moving showed me I could be rebuilt, that I was more portable than I'd feared. The boxes are long gone, and what I carried was never in them.

# Dust Bowl

The Dust Bowl, also known as the Dirty Thirties, was a period of severe dust storms that caused major ecological and agricultural damage to the American and Canadian prairie lands during the 1930s. Severe drought and decades of extensive farming without techniques to prevent wind erosion, such as crop rotation, cover crops, and terracing, caused it.

## Background

During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, settlers moved onto the Great Plains in large numbers, encouraged by the Homestead Acts and by unusually wet weather in the early 1900s. The native deep-rooted prairie grasses were plowed under to plant wheat. High wheat prices during and after World War I accelerated this expansion, and gasoline-powered tractors and combines let farmers cultivate far more land than before. Millions of acres of grassland became cropland, leaving the soil exposed.

## Drought and storms

A series of droughts began in 1930 and recurred in waves through 1936 and again in 1939 and 1940. With the grasses that once anchored the soil gone, high winds lifted the dry topsoil into enormous clouds. The most severe region included the panhandles of Texas and Oklahoma, as well as parts of western Kansas, eastern Colorado, and northeastern New Mexico.

On April 14, 1935, remembered as "Black Sunday," a massive storm carried dust across the southern plains, turning day into night. The following day, journalist Robert Geiger used the term "Dust Bowl" in a news dispatch, and the name endured. Some storms carried dust as far as Washington, D.C., and ships in the Atlantic Ocean.

## Human impact

The storms damaged crops, buried farm equipment, and killed livestock. Many residents developed "dust pneumonia" and other respiratory illnesses. Together with the economic hardship of the Great Depression, the crisis forced many families to leave their farms. Roughly 3.5 million people moved out of the Plains states in the 1930s, many of them heading to California. John Steinbeck's novel *The Grapes of Wrath* (1939), Dorothea Lange's photographs, and Woody Guthrie's songs all recorded their experiences.

## Government response

The federal government set up programs to address the crisis. The Soil Conservation Service, created in 1935 under Hugh Hammond Bennett, promoted soil-saving techniques including contour plowing, strip cropping, and crop rotation. The Prairie States Forestry Project, begun in 1934, planted millions of trees across the Plains as windbreaks known as shelterbelts. The Taylor Grazing Act of 1934 also regulated grazing on public lands.

## Legacy

Rainfall returned in late 1939, ending the drought. The Dust Bowl is one of the worst environmental disasters in American history, and it changed soil conservation policy and farming practices.

The Erie Canal is a canal in New York State that cut the cost of shipping goods across the United States in the 19th century. It opened in 1825 and gave boats a water route from the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo, linking the Atlantic Ocean with the Great Lakes. Freight became much cheaper to move, settlers reached the west faster, and New York City became the nation's leading port.

The canal was proposed in the early 19th century because moving goods and people across the Appalachians was slow, expensive, and often unreliable. Governor DeWitt Clinton became its leading political backer, and critics mockingly called the project "Clinton's Ditch." Construction began in 1817. Thousands of laborers, many of them immigrants, cut through forests, dug trenches, and built aqueducts and locks across difficult terrain.

The original canal was about 363 miles (584 km) long, 40 feet (12 m) wide, and 4 feet (1.2 m) deep. Its 83 locks carried boats over an elevation difference of more than 500 feet (150 m) between the Hudson and Lake Erie. It officially opened on October 26, 1825. To mark the day, Clinton made the trip from Buffalo to New York Harbor and poured water from Lake Erie into the Atlantic, a ceremony called the "Wedding of the Waters."

Freight rates between the Midwest and the East Coast fell sharply, so farm products, raw materials, and manufactured goods all became cheaper to ship. Syracuse, Rochester, Utica, and Buffalo grew rapidly along the route. The canal also drew settlers to western New York, Ohio, Indiana, and other parts of the Old Northwest.

Because the canal did so well, it was enlarged several times during the 19th century. In 1918, much of the original route became part of the New York State Barge Canal System, which used both canalized rivers and new canal cuts. Railroads and highways later took most of its commercial traffic.

Today the canal is used mainly for recreation, tourism, and historic preservation.

Learning a second language as an adult showed me that intelligence is humbler than I used to think. Before I started, I imagined it would test my memory and discipline, and maybe my talent. I thought that if I worked hard enough, I would climb steadily from confusion to fluency, collecting grammar rules and vocabulary the way you collect tools. Instead, it felt like becoming a beginner again.

As a child, I never noticed how much of life runs on language. I moved through my first language without thinking about it. I joked, apologized, complained, and told stories as naturally as breathing. But when I started on another language as an adult, even the simplest exchanges got heavy. I could have a thought in full color and then find I only had the words to express it in black and white. A personality that felt quick and articulate in one language turned hesitant and simple in another. It startled me to see how much of what I called "myself" depended on ease of expression.

It made me more patient, with myself and with other people. When you struggle to ask where the bathroom is, or order the wrong food, or misunderstand a question and answer confidently anyway, you get more generous about how people communicate. I started to see how brave it is to live, work, and raise a family in a language that isn't fully yours. Before, I admired bilingualism in the abstract. Now I see it as daily courage.

I also learned that embarrassment is survivable. Adults tend to avoid anything that makes them look foolish. Children have no choice, so they are constantly corrected, misunderstood, and exposed, and they keep going. Adults guard their competence like a fragile possession. Learning the language made me speak badly, pronounce things wrong, forget words I had "already learned," and hear the limits of my own mouth and memory. At first that was frustrating. Eventually it was freeing. Improvement depends less on avoiding mistakes than on putting up with them.

The biggest surprise was how it changed my listening. In my native language I mostly listen for meaning. In a second language I listen for structure, tone, rhythm, and intention, and I notice what is said, what is implied, and what I might have missed. That habit began carrying over into my first language. I became slower to assume and quicker to ask, and I understood better that following another person is never as automatic as it seems.

Growth is often awkward, humility turns out to be useful, and communication is both more fragile and more generous than I used to think. Being a beginner again made me pay attention.

I also learned that embarrassment is survivable. Adults tend to avoid anything that makes them look foolish. Children have no choice, so they are constantly corrected, misunderstood, and exposed, and they keep going. Adults guard their competence like a fragile possession. Learning the language made me speak badly, pronounce things wrong, forget words I had "already learned," and hear the limits of my own mouth and memory. At first that was frustrating. Eventually it was freeing. Improvement depends less on avoiding mistakes than on putting up with them.

The biggest surprise was how it changed my listening. In my native language I mostly listen for meaning. In a second language I listen for structure, tone, rhythm, and intention, and I notice what is said, what is implied, and what I might have missed. That habit began carrying over into my first language. I became slower to assume and quicker to ask, and I understood better that following another person is never as automatic as it seems.

Growth is often awkward, humility turns out to be useful, and communication is both more fragile and more generous than I used to think. Being a beginner again made me pay attention.

**Record turnout in Riverton school-board election**

Voters turned out in record numbers Tuesday for the Riverton School Board election.

According to the Riverton County Elections Office, more than 18,400 ballots were cast, about 46 percent of registered voters in the district. Officials said it was the highest turnout ever recorded for a stand-alone school-board election in the community, beating the 2017 record by nearly 5,000 votes.

Election workers reported steady lines at polling sites across the district all day, heaviest in the morning and again after work. Early and absentee voting also rose sharply.

"This is the kind of civic engagement every local government hopes to see," said County Elections Director Marisol Vega. "School-board elections typically bring in a smaller slice of the electorate, so this level of turnout is remarkable."

The turnout followed months of public debate over school funding, classroom overcrowding, campus safety, and the direction of the district's curriculum. Candidate forums drew large audiences, and community groups on all sides ran outreach campaigns urging residents to vote.

Three seats were open. Incumbent Daniel Harper kept his, and newcomers Alicia Gomez and Trent Wallace appeared headed for victory based on unofficial returns released Tuesday night. Certified results are expected later this week, though the margins were wide enough that observers said the outcome was unlikely to change.

Supporters of the winning candidates called the result a clear message from voters that the district needs both stability and fresh ideas. "People care deeply about what happens in our schools," Gomez told supporters at a gathering Tuesday evening. "Tonight's turnout shows this community is paying attention and wants a voice in the decisions affecting students and families."

Residents did not all read the results the same way, but many said the number of voters was encouraging. Parents, teachers, and retirees interviewed outside polling sites said the school board has an outsized effect on daily life, from academic standards to bus routes and extracurricular programs.

Superintendent Karen Liu said the election showed broad public investment in the district's future. "Regardless of who people supported, it is heartening to see so many residents participate," Liu said. "That kind of involvement strengthens public education."

Local analysts said the turnout suggests school-board races can draw voters when the issues feel immediate and personal, which could change how future elections play out.

# Startup Recalls Faulty Home Battery After Overheating Reports

A fast-growing home energy startup has issued a voluntary recall of one of its residential battery systems after reports that a defect could cause the unit to overheat, raising concerns about fire risk in homes where the product was installed.

The company, VoltNest Energy, said Tuesday that it is recalling about 8,200 units of its PowerVault S1 battery, a wall-mounted system that stores electricity from rooftop solar panels or provides backup power during outages. The batteries were sold in the United States between March 2024 and September 2026 through solar installers and the company's website.

In a statement, VoltNest said it had received 27 reports of overheating. Five involved minor property damage, such as scorched walls and melted wiring insulation. No serious injuries have been reported, though two customers sought medical evaluation for possible smoke inhalation.

The startup said the problem appears to come from a manufacturing defect in a batch of lithium iron phosphate battery modules from a third-party vendor. Under certain charging conditions, an internal component can fail and potentially cause excessive heat buildup.

"We are acting out of an abundance of caution," VoltNest Chief Executive Maya Levin said in the statement. "Customer safety is our top priority, and we are working closely with regulators, installers and homeowners to replace affected units as quickly as possible."

Customers are advised to shut down the battery immediately using the system's main disconnect switch and not to try repairing or removing it themselves. VoltNest said it will provide free inspections, software diagnostics and unit replacements where necessary. It has also released a firmware update meant to reduce charging stress until replacements are carried out, but said the update does not replace the recall.

The recall was announced in coordination with the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, which urged owners to follow the company's shutdown instructions and contact VoltNest or their installer. The agency said recalled units can be identified by serial numbers beginning with PVS1-24 or PVS1-25.

VoltNest is a venture-backed startup that has positioned itself as a lower-cost rival in the home battery market. Founded in 2021, it has expanded quickly as demand for residential backup power has grown amid more frequent extreme weather and strain on electric grids.

Industry analysts said the recall could slow the company's momentum for a while, and that its handling of the response may matter more than the defect itself.

"Recalls are damaging, especially for a young brand," said energy storage analyst Daniel Cho. "But in this industry, transparency and speed matter. Homeowners need confidence that these systems are safe inside their garages and utility rooms."

# Svalbard Global Seed Vault

The **Svalbard Global Seed Vault** (Norwegian: *Svalbard globale frøhvelv*) is a secure backup facility for the world's crop diversity, located on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen in the Svalbard archipelago. It is often called the "Doomsday Vault" in the media. It stores duplicate samples of seeds held in gene banks around the world, as insurance against the loss of collections through accident, mismanagement, war, or natural disaster.

## History

The vault was proposed in the 1980s and gained momentum through the work of agricultural scientist Cary Fowler, who later led the Global Crop Diversity Trust (now the Crop Trust). The Norwegian government funded construction, which cost approximately NOK 50 million. The facility opened on 26 February 2008.

## Location and design

The vault is built into a sandstone mountain near Longyearbyen, about 1,300 kilometres from the North Pole, and sits roughly 130 metres above sea level. This elevation was chosen to keep it above any projected sea-level rise. A tunnel about 120 metres long leads to three storage chambers, each designed to hold up to 1.5 million seed samples. The total capacity is 4.5 million varieties, or about 2.25 billion seeds.

The surrounding permafrost provides natural cooling, and refrigeration keeps the chambers at about −18 °C, the standard temperature for long-term seed storage. At that temperature and low moisture, the seeds of many major crops can remain viable for centuries or longer. The site was also selected for its geological stability and low level of tectonic activity.

## Operation

The vault is owned by the Norwegian government and managed in cooperation with the Crop Trust and the Nordic Genetic Resource Center (NordGen). Storage is free of charge, with costs covered by Norway and the Crop Trust. Depositing institutions retain ownership of their samples, which are stored in sealed foil packages in boxes that no one else may open. The vault is only a backup, and only depositors may withdraw their material.

By the early 2020s, the collection held more than 1.2 million samples from nearly every country, including varieties of rice, wheat, maize, barley, sorghum, and many regional crops.

## Notable events

In 2015, the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) made the first major withdrawal, requesting copies of seeds originally held in Aleppo, Syria, after the Syrian civil war disrupted its gene bank operations. The center used them to re-establish collections in Morocco and Lebanon.

In 2017, unusually warm weather and heavy rain caused meltwater to enter the entrance tunnel. The seeds were not affected, but Norway subsequently funded substantial upgrades, including waterproofing and improved drainage.

## Significance

The vault is widely seen as a symbol of international cooperation on food security and biodiversity conservation. The 2017 meltwater incident also showed that climate change can threaten facilities built to withstand long-term risks.

I have never trusted any habit that arrives with too much ceremony. The ones that save me tend to be small and a little shy: making coffee before I am fully awake, opening a window in winter, walking for no particular reason. Walking is the one I depend on most. It asks the least of me and gives back the most.

For a long time I did not think of walking as a practice. It was what happened between places: errands, late buses, parking two streets away, crossing campus in bad weather. It was practical, forgettable, and often slightly annoying. Somewhere along the way it stopped being a delay before life and started to feel like part of it.

Part of its comfort is how undramatic it is. Walking needs no talent, special equipment, or right mood, and it does not ask me to improve myself. On days when I am tired, restless, or vaguely discontented in the modern way, with too much screen and too many tabs open in my mind, I can still put on shoes and go outside. Much of contemporary life is frictionless in the wrong ways: messages arrive instantly, news follows me from room to room, whole afternoons disappear while my body stays still. Walking brings back a useful kind of friction. Distance is real, weather is real, my legs are real.

My thoughts behave differently when I walk. At a desk, problems harden and take on the dense, airless quality of something overhandled. On a walk, even familiar worries loosen. The rhythm of steps gives the mind just enough to do that it stops gripping so tightly. I have had ideas arrive while crossing intersections, remembered lines I thought were lost, forgiven people a little, forgiven myself a little. None of this feels mystical. Movement changes the scale of thought. What seemed inescapable indoors becomes, outside, one thing among many: a barking dog, a passing train, the smell of cut grass, the sudden authority of a tree.

Walking also returns me to my senses. The world starts to feel like company. The same street is never exactly the same street. There are seasonal revisions: wet leaves plastered to the sidewalk, the medicinal brightness of cold air, the exhausted abundance of late summer gardens. There are tiny neighborhood dramas: a child chalking suns on the pavement, someone learning to ride a bicycle, a curtain lifted and dropped. To walk regularly is to become a modest witness. You learn the habits of dogs, the timing of sprinklers, where the first crocuses insist on appearing. Familiarity accumulates, and with it a quiet affection.

What I value most is that walking offers progress that cannot be optimized into meaninglessness. One foot in front of the other is both an instruction and a philosophy. You do not have to leap or finish everything today. You move, you pause, you continue. There is humility in that, and relief.

When I return from a walk, my life is usually unchanged in any measurable way. The emails are still there, and so are the unanswered questions. But I feel slightly rejoined to myself. The world extends beyond my preoccupations, and I can meet it with my own body, at a human pace. For such an ordinary habit, walking does a great deal: it brings me back to proportion, which more and more feels like a kind of grace.

## Create calendar event

Creates a new event on a user's calendar.

### Endpoint

`POST /v1/events`

### Description

Use this endpoint to create a calendar event with a title, start time, and end time. Optional fields include description, location, attendees, reminders, recurrence, and time zone. On success, the API returns the newly created event object, including its unique identifier.

### Authentication

Requires a valid bearer token:

```http
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
```

### Request headers

| Header | Type | Required | Description |
|--------|------|----------|-------------|
| Authorization | string | Yes | Bearer access token |
| Content-Type | string | Yes | Must be `application/json` |

### Request body

```json
{
  "title": "Team Sync",
  "start": "2026-11-20T09:00:00Z",
  "end": "2026-11-20T09:30:00Z",
  "description": "Weekly project status meeting",
  "location": "Conference Room A",
  "timezone": "UTC",
  "attendees": [
    "alex@example.com",
    "sam@example.com"
  ],
  "reminders": [
    {
      "method": "email",
      "minutesBefore": 30
    }
  ],
  "recurrence": {
    "frequency": "weekly",
    "interval": 1
  }
}
```

### Body parameters

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|------|------|----------|-------------|
| title | string | Yes | Event title, max 200 characters |
| start | string | Yes | Start date/time in ISO 8601 format |
| end | string | Yes | End date/time in ISO 8601 format |
| description | string | No | Event details, max 5000 characters |
| location | string | No | Event location |
| timezone | string | No | IANA time zone, e.g. `America/New_York` |
| attendees | array[string] | No | List of attendee email addresses |
| reminders | array[object] | No | Reminder definitions |
| reminders[].method | string | Yes | `email` or `popup` |
| reminders[].minutesBefore | integer | Yes | Minutes before event start |
| recurrence | object | No | Recurrence settings |
| recurrence.frequency | string | No | `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly`, or `yearly` |
| recurrence.interval | integer | No | Repeat interval, must be greater than 0 |

### Response

201 Created

```json
{
  "id": "evt_01J9X8K7M2R4A6P9",
  "title": "Team Sync",
  "start": "2026-11-20T09:00:00Z",
  "end": "2026-11-20T09:30:00Z",
  "description": "Weekly project status meeting",
  "location": "Conference Room A",
  "timezone": "UTC",
  "attendees": [
    "alex@example.com",
    "sam@example.com"
  ],
  "status": "confirmed",
  "createdAt": "2026-11-10T14:22:31Z"
}
```

### Error responses

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| 400 Bad Request | Missing required fields, invalid JSON, or malformed dates |
| 401 Unauthorized | Missing or invalid access token |
| 403 Forbidden | Token does not have permission to create events |
| 409 Conflict | Event overlaps with a protected calendar block |
| 422 Unprocessable Entity | Validation failed, such as `end` occurring before `start` |

Example error:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "validation_error",
    "message": "The `end` time must be later than `start`."
  }
}
```

### Notes

- All timestamps must use ISO 8601 format.
- If `timezone` is omitted, the calendar's default time zone is used.
- Attendees may receive invitations depending on account settings.
- A recurring event may create a series instead of a single event.

# Cyberattack at Riverbend Health exposes records of nearly 380,000 patients

Hospital network says names, Social Security numbers and treatment details were accessed; investigators believe attackers were inside systems for three weeks

RIVERBEND, Ohio. Riverbend Health, a regional network of seven hospitals and more than 40 outpatient clinics, confirmed Tuesday that attackers gained unauthorized access to its systems and may have stolen personal and medical information belonging to approximately 378,000 current and former patients.

In a statement posted to its website, the network said it discovered suspicious activity on March 4 after IT staff noticed unusual data transfers from a server used to store billing records. The network said the intruders appear to have had access since mid-February.

"We deeply regret this incident and the concern it causes our patients," said Dr. Elaine Marchetti, Riverbend Health's chief executive. "Protecting patient information is central to our mission, and we are taking every step to understand what happened and prevent it from happening again."

According to the network, the compromised data may include names, birth dates, home addresses, Social Security numbers, insurance information, and details of diagnoses and treatments. Riverbend said it found no evidence that the attackers accessed its electronic health record system, which holds full clinical charts, though the investigation is ongoing.

Emergency departments remained open during the incident, but the network confirmed that some scheduling and billing systems were taken offline for nearly a week. Several patients reported rescheduled appointments and delayed test results.

"I showed up for a follow-up and they were writing everything on paper," said Dana Whitfield, 54, who receives care at a Riverbend cardiology clinic. "Now I'm worried about who has my information."

Riverbend has hired an outside cybersecurity firm and notified the FBI and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, which maintains a public list of large healthcare breaches. The network said it has not received a ransom demand, though a ransomware group has claimed responsibility on a dark web leak site and posted what it says are sample files. Riverbend said it is reviewing those claims.

Healthcare organizations remain frequent targets because medical records combine many kinds of data that can be used for identity theft and fraud, security experts say.

"A stolen credit card can be canceled in minutes. A Social Security number and medical history can be exploited for years," said Raymond Okafor, a health care cybersecurity consultant not involved in the investigation.

Riverbend will begin mailing notification letters next week and is offering two years of free credit monitoring and identity theft protection. Patients can call a dedicated hotline at 1-800-555-0142.

# Cyberattack at Riverbend Health exposes records of nearly 380,000 patients

Hospital network says names, Social Security numbers and treatment details were accessed; investigators believe attackers were inside systems for three weeks

RIVERBEND, Ohio. Riverbend Health, a regional network of seven hospitals and more than 40 outpatient clinics, confirmed Tuesday that attackers gained unauthorized access to its systems and may have stolen personal and medical information belonging to approximately 378,000 current and former patients.

In a statement posted to its website, the network said it discovered suspicious activity on March 4 after IT staff noticed unusual data transfers from a server used to store billing records. The network said the intruders appear to have had access since mid-February.

"We deeply regret this incident and the concern it causes our patients," said Dr. Elaine Marchetti, Riverbend Health's chief executive. "Protecting patient information is central to our mission, and we are taking every step to understand what happened and prevent it from happening again."

According to the network, the compromised data may include names, birth dates, home addresses, Social Security numbers, insurance information, and details of diagnoses and treatments. Riverbend said it found no evidence that the attackers accessed its electronic health record system, which holds full clinical charts, though the investigation is ongoing.

Emergency departments remained open during the incident, but the network confirmed that some scheduling and billing systems were taken offline for nearly a week. Several patients reported rescheduled appointments and delayed test results.

"I showed up for a follow-up and they were writing everything on paper," said Dana Whitfield, 54, who receives care at a Riverbend cardiology clinic. "Now I'm worried about who has my information."

Riverbend has hired an outside cybersecurity firm and notified the FBI and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, which maintains a public list of large healthcare breaches. The network said it has not received a ransom demand, though a ransomware group has claimed responsibility on a dark web leak site and posted what it says are sample files. Riverbend said it is reviewing those claims.

Healthcare organizations remain frequent targets because medical records combine many kinds of data that can be used for identity theft and fraud, security experts say.

"A stolen credit card can be canceled in minutes. A Social Security number and medical history can be exploited for years," said Raymond Okafor, a health care cybersecurity consultant not involved in the investigation.

# Antikythera mechanism

The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient Greek hand-powered orrery, often described as the earliest known analog computer. It was used to predict astronomical positions and eclipses decades in advance, and to track the cycles of the Greek calendar, including the timing of major Panhellenic games. The device is generally dated to the 2nd or 1st century BCE.

## Discovery

The mechanism was recovered in 1901 from a Roman-era shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera, between Kythera and Crete. Sponge divers found the wreck in 1900, and salvage operations led by the Greek Navy and archaeologists brought up statues, pottery, jewelry, coins, and a corroded lump of bronze. The lump was later found to contain gears and inscriptions. It is now held at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

## Construction

The device was housed in a wooden case roughly the size of a shoebox. Its bronze components, many of them thin and finely cut, survive in 82 known fragments. Turning a crank drove a system of at least 30 interlocking gears with triangular teeth, which moved pointers across dials on the front and back of the case.

The front dial showed the positions of the Sun and Moon in the zodiac, along with a calendar. A small rotating, partly silvered ball displayed the Moon's phase. The back had two large spiral dials: one for the Metonic cycle (19 years, matching solar years to lunar months) and one for the Saros cycle (about 18 years, used to predict eclipses). Smaller subsidiary dials tracked other cycles, including the Callippic cycle and the Olympiad cycle.

The Moon's irregular motion, caused by its elliptical orbit, was modeled with a pin-and-slot mechanism using two gears with offset axes. This matches the lunar theory attributed to Hipparchus.

## Research

Valerios Stais, and later Derek de Solla Price from the 1950s through the 1970s, established the device's basic function. X-ray imaging in the 1970s and the Antikythera Mechanism Research Project, begun in 2005, then read much of the inscriptions using microfocus X-ray computed tomography and surface imaging. The inscriptions amount to a user's manual. Researchers have also proposed that the device displayed planetary positions, and reconstructions of such gearing have been published, though the evidence remains incomplete.

## Significance

No surviving artifact shows comparable sophistication for over a thousand years, until medieval astronomical clocks in Europe and the Islamic world. Its origin is debated, with possible links to Rhodes, Corinth, or Syracuse, and to the traditions of Hipparchus or Archimedes.

# Photo Date Renamer

A command-line tool that renames photo files after the date they were taken, read from EXIF metadata. Photo libraries become easier to sort and search, and easier to archive across folders and devices.

## Features

- Renames photos using the original capture date from EXIF metadata
- Supports JPG and JPEG files
- Produces consistent, sortable filenames
- Appends a counter when two photos share a timestamp
- Works on a single folder or recursively through subfolders
- Has a dry-run mode that previews changes before any file is renamed

## Why use it?

Cameras and phones name files things like `IMG_4032.JPG` or `DSC00123.jpg`, which stop being useful once the files land in a larger collection. This tool replaces those names with timestamp-based ones:

```bash
2023-08-14_18-42-09.jpg
2023-08-14_18-42-09_2.jpg
```

Names in this format sort in date order, and they make it easier to merge photos from several devices.

## Installation

Clone the repository and install the dependencies:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/yourname/photo-date-renamer.git
cd photo-date-renamer
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

If the package is published, you can also install it with:

```bash
pip install photo-date-renamer
```

## Usage

Rename all supported photos in a folder:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos
```

Process folders recursively:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --recursive
```

Preview changes without modifying files:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --dry-run
```

Use a custom filename format:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --format "%Y/%m/%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S"
```

## Filename behavior

By default, files are renamed with this pattern:

```text
YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS.ext
```

Examples:

- `IMG_0001.JPG` becomes `2022-05-06_14-33-21.jpg`
- `DSC7788.jpeg` becomes `2022-05-06_14-33-21_2.jpeg`

If two or more photos share the same timestamp, the tool adds a numeric suffix so no file is overwritten.

## Missing metadata

If a file has no valid capture date in its EXIF metadata, the tool skips it and lists it in the summary. A future version may let you fall back to the file's creation or modification time.

## Safety

- Warns before it would overwrite an existing file
- Previews changes with a dry run
- Reports renamed, skipped, and failed files when it finishes

## Example output

```bash
Renamed: IMG_1203.JPG -> 2021-11-03_09-15-44.jpg
Renamed: IMG_1204.JPG -> 2021-11-03_09-15-45.jpg
Skipped: scan_01.jpg (no EXIF date found)

Done. 2 renamed, 1 skipped, 0 failed.
```

## Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome. To report a bug or suggest a feature, open an issue with sample filenames, the behavior you expected, and your platform.

## License

MIT License.

**Regional Airline Cancels Dozens of Flights Amid Pilot Shortage**

A regional airline has cancelled dozens of flights this week, citing a shortage of qualified pilots. The cancellations have disrupted schedules and left passengers scrambling to make other travel arrangements.

The carrier, which flies short-haul routes between smaller cities and major hubs, said it had to cancel flights to stay within federal crew-rest and staffing requirements. Officials said staffing had fallen below what was needed to operate the full schedule reliably.

"We regret the inconvenience to our customers, but safety remains our top priority," the airline said in a statement released Tuesday. "Like many regional carriers across the industry, we are facing significant challenges in recruiting and retaining pilots."

The cancellations hit routes in several states, and some passengers learned only hours before departure that their flights had been pulled. At several regional airports, travelers reported long lines at customer service desks while staff rebooked customers on later flights or arranged ground transportation.

"I was supposed to fly out this morning for a business meeting, and now the next available flight isn't until tomorrow," said one passenger at a regional airport. "It's frustrating because there weren't many backup options."

Industry analysts say pilot shortages have become a growing problem for regional airlines, which often serve as a training ground for pilots before they move to larger, better-paying mainline carriers. Regionals have struggled to compete on wages and quality of life, especially as demand for air travel has rebounded and larger airlines have expanded hiring.

Mandatory retirement rules, higher training costs, and stricter experience requirements for new pilots have made it worse. Together they have narrowed the pool of available crew, particularly for smaller carriers in less profitable markets.

Aviation consultant Mark Ellison said regional airlines are often hit hardest because they have fewer staffing reserves. "When a major airline loses a few pilots, it can sometimes absorb that disruption," he said. "For a regional carrier, even a small staffing gap can force widespread cancellations."

The airline said it is offering travel waivers and refunds to affected customers and is working to restore normal operations as quickly as possible. It said it is also hiring, with recruitment bonuses and expanded training partnerships.

Local business leaders and airport officials in communities that depend on regional service warn that prolonged reductions could hurt tourism, business travel, and the local economy.

Passengers should check flight status before heading to the airport, since further schedule changes are possible in the coming days.

# Wildfire forces evacuations near Redwood Canyon National Park

REDWOOD COUNTY, Calif. A fast-moving wildfire near Redwood Canyon National Park forced mandatory evacuations Tuesday. Officials said dry conditions, gusty winds and rugged terrain were fueling the blaze.

The Canyon Ridge Fire started late Monday afternoon about five miles east of the park's southern boundary. By Tuesday evening it had grown to an estimated 7,800 acres, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection. Containment remained low as crews worked to protect homes, campgrounds and critical infrastructure in nearby mountain communities.

Authorities ordered residents of the small towns of Pine Creek, Alder Grove and Millstone to leave, along with several rural neighborhoods along Highway 86. An evacuation warning was also issued for parts of the park's gateway communities, where visitors were urged to be ready to leave on short notice.

"This fire is moving rapidly and conditions can change minute by minute," Incident Commander Laura Mendes said during an evening briefing. "Our top priority is life safety: getting people out of harm's way and giving firefighters the room they need to work."

As of Tuesday night, no deaths or serious injuries had been reported. Officials said several structures were threatened and at least two outbuildings had been destroyed. The cause of the fire is under investigation.

A section of Highway 86 was closed to non-emergency traffic. Park officials closed the southern entrance temporarily, along with several backcountry trails and campgrounds. Rangers began escorting campers out of affected areas early Tuesday, while smoke settled over nearby valleys and reduced visibility across the region.

The National Weather Service issued a red flag warning for the area, citing low humidity, high temperatures and wind gusts that could exceed 30 mph. Fire officials said those conditions were expected to last into Wednesday and would make containment harder.

More than 600 firefighters were assigned to the fire, with air tankers, helicopters and bulldozers in support. Crews worked overnight to cut containment lines and protect structures in the evacuation zones.

At an evacuation center at Redwood County High School, displaced residents gathered with pets, medications and a few belongings. Volunteers handed out food, water and blankets while families waited for updates.

"We grabbed what we could and left," said Pine Creek resident Maria Lopez, who evacuated with her husband and two children. "You could see the glow on the ridge, and the wind was just pushing it closer."

Officials urged residents to monitor emergency alerts and stay away from the area. "If you have been told to leave, leave now," Mendes said. "Do not wait to see the fire."

# Commit message style guide

A good commit message says what changed and why, so future readers can follow the history without reading every diff. Keep messages short and consistent.

## Structure

Use this format:

```text
<type>: <short summary>

<optional body>

<optional footer>
```

### 1. Short summary

- Keep it to 50 characters or fewer when possible.
- Use the imperative mood: "add", "fix", "remove", not "added" or "fixes".
- Start with a lowercase type followed by a colon.
- Do not end the summary with a period.

Examples:
- `fix: handle null response in user service`
- `docs: clarify local setup steps`
- `refactor: simplify cache invalidation logic`

### 2. Body

Use the body when the summary alone does not make the change obvious.

Guidelines:
- Wrap lines at about 72 characters.
- Explain why the change was made before describing implementation details.
- Include context, tradeoffs, side effects, or migration notes if relevant.
- Use short paragraphs or bullet points for readability.

A useful pattern:
- What problem existed?
- Why was this approach chosen?
- Are there risks or follow-up tasks?

### 3. Footer

Use footers for metadata when needed:
- Issue references: `Refs: #123`
- Closing references: `Closes: #456`
- Breaking changes: `BREAKING CHANGE: config format has changed`

## Recommended types

Pick a small, predictable set of types. Common ones include:
- `feat`: new functionality
- `fix`: bug fix
- `docs`: documentation only
- `refactor`: code change without behavior change
- `test`: tests added or updated
- `chore`: maintenance, tooling, dependency updates
- `perf`: performance improvement
- `build`: build system or dependency management changes
- `ci`: continuous integration changes

## Best practices

- Make each commit one logical change.
- Write the message as if giving a command:
  - "add validation for empty emails"
  - "remove deprecated API client"
- Be specific. Prefer:
  - `fix: prevent duplicate invoice creation`

  over:
  - `fix: bug fixes`
- If a commit is large or complex, explain it.
- Review the message before committing, because it becomes part of the permanent project history.

## Avoid

- Vague summaries like `update stuff` or `misc fixes`
- Overly long subjects
- Describing only the code, not the reason
- Combining unrelated changes in one commit
- Auto-generated messages left unedited, such as `WIP` or `temp`

## Example

```text
fix: prevent retry loop on expired auth token

The client kept retrying requests after receiving a 401 response,
which caused unnecessary traffic and delayed user-facing errors.

Stop retries when the token is expired and surface a re-auth
prompt instead.

Closes: #214
```

Consistency matters more than perfection. A shared standard is enough to keep the history searchable.

## Installation

This library requires Python 3.8 or later and is a standard Python package.

Install it with `pip`:

```bash
pip install csvparser
```

Inside a project, create a virtual environment first:

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate      # macOS / Linux
.venv\Scripts\activate         # Windows
pip install csvparser
```

To confirm the installation:

```bash
python -c "import csvparser; print(csvparser.__version__)"
```

To install from source, clone the repository and install in editable mode:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/your-org/csvparser.git
cd csvparser
pip install -e .
```

Editable mode picks up local code changes immediately, so you don't have to reinstall while developing.

## Quick start

In the most basic case, you load a file and iterate through its rows as dictionaries.

Suppose you have a file named `people.csv`:

```csv
name,age,city
Alice,30,London
Bob,25,Paris
Charlie,35,Berlin
```

You can parse it like this:

```python
from csvparser import CSVParser

parser = CSVParser("people.csv")
rows = parser.read()

for row in rows:
    print(row)
```

Output:

```python
{'name': 'Alice', 'age': '30', 'city': 'London'}
{'name': 'Bob', 'age': '25', 'city': 'Paris'}
{'name': 'Charlie', 'age': '35', 'city': 'Berlin'}
```

### Reading rows one at a time

For large files, iterate over the parser instead of loading everything into memory:

```python
from csvparser import CSVParser

parser = CSVParser("people.csv")

for row in parser:
    print(row["name"], row["city"])
```

### Custom delimiter

If your file uses a delimiter other than a comma, pass it when you create the parser:

```python
parser = CSVParser("data.tsv", delimiter="\t")
rows = parser.read()
```

### Header validation

To require specific column names, pass `required_columns`:

```python
parser = CSVParser(
    "people.csv",
    required_columns=["name", "age", "city"]
)

rows = parser.read()
```

If a required column is missing, the parser raises an error right away, before any rows are processed.

**The Fifth Day**

For six years I spent Sunday evenings in a low hum of dread. Nothing was wrong, exactly. The job was fine, the colleagues were kind. But the weekend had a way of evaporating. Saturday went to errands and recovery, Sunday to anticipating Monday. I was always living in the margins of my own life.

Then my company ran a pilot: four days a week, same pay, same expectations of output. I assumed it was a trick. I figured I'd either work ten-hour days or come back to a mountain of Friday's undone tasks.

What happened was stranger. The work shrank to fit the time. Meetings that had wandered for an hour found their point in twenty minutes. We stopped scheduling gatherings to discuss other gatherings. When you only have four days, you protect them. People started saying no more often, and, oddly, everything important still got done.

The research since has echoed what I felt. In the 2022 UK pilot, which involved about 61 companies and roughly 2,900 workers, the large majority of firms kept the shorter week afterward. Employees reported less burnout and better sleep, and revenue held steady. Iceland's earlier trials told a similar story. None of this proves every workplace could do it, but it undercuts the assumption that more hours automatically means more value.

I think that assumption does the most damage. We inherited the five-day week from an industrial era when output tracked hours on the factory floor. Most of us no longer work that way. Knowledge work runs on attention, and attention doesn't scale linearly. The fifth day was often the one where I was physically present but mentally gone, answering emails to prove I existed.

Rest mattered, but what I got back was mostly ordinary life. I went to the dentist without negotiating a calendar. I cooked a real dinner on a Friday. I spent a long afternoon with my father, who is older than he used to be, and I noticed how much of our relationship had been conducted in scraps of leftover time. A day off gives you room for the things that make a person more than an employee.

Critics worry about fairness, and they're right to. A four-day week is harder to arrange for nurses, teachers, and restaurant staff, whose work can't be compressed by cutting meetings. But that's an argument for designing it thoughtfully, with staggered shifts, more hiring, and honest measurement, and it doesn't justify refusing to try it where it works. Some people will also compress five days into four longer ones, which misses the point. The goal is fewer hours, spent well.

I don't think the four-day week will fix everything. Bad managers will remain bad, and pressure will find new outlets. But I came back from that pilot with a clearer sense of what work is for: it's a part of life, and it shouldn't be what the rest of life is organized around.

These days, Sunday evenings are quiet. I notice that more than any productivity statistic.

# The Teacher Who Waited

In seventh grade, I had a math teacher named Mr. Okafor who did something I found infuriating at the time: he refused to give me the answer.

I was stuck on a word problem about two trains, and I raised my hand with the confidence of someone who believed adults existed to resolve confusion quickly. He walked over, looked at my paper, and asked, "What do you know so far?" I said I knew nothing. He said, "Great. Let's write that down." Then he waited, with no sigh and no sign of impatience, like a man with all afternoon. Eventually, to fill the silence, I began listing things: the trains left at different times, one was faster. Somewhere in the middle of my own sentence, I saw it.

I've thought about that silence for years. It taught me something counterintuitive about good teachers: the goal of teaching is to build a person who can find knowledge on their own.

Knowing the material matters, of course. A teacher who doesn't understand the subject can't guide anyone through it. But I've met brilliant people who were terrible teachers because they'd forgotten what it felt like not to know. Expertise can make you impatient with confusion. Mr. Okafor seemed to treat confusion as a natural, even interesting, place to stand. He never made me feel stupid for being there.

That, I think, is the second quality: a good teacher makes it safe to be wrong. In his classroom, mistakes went on the board as public property, and he examined them with curiosity. "Interesting," he'd say. "Where did this go sideways?" We learned to hunt our own errors like detectives instead of hiding them like evidence. I've carried that into adulthood, where admitting a mistake early is often the difference between a small problem and a catastrophic one.

The third quality is harder to describe. Good teachers believe in you slightly before you've earned it. Mr. Okafor once handed me a problem from a competition packet meant for older students and said, "I think you'd enjoy this one." I didn't solve it. But I spent a week trying, and I remember the feeling of being taken seriously. His expectation was a kind of loan, and I worked hard to repay it.

I've since had teachers who were more charismatic and more celebrated, and some of them were wonderful. But when I think about who changed how I think, I return to the man who stood beside my desk and let a silence stretch until I filled it myself.

It takes real restraint to teach this way. It would have been faster to show me the solution, and I'd have been grateful for about ten minutes. Instead he gave me something slower and longer lasting: the experience of figuring it out, and the quiet discovery that I could.

I don't remember the answer to the train problem, but I remember the waiting.

# Regional Airline Cancels Dozens of Flights as Pilot Shortage Deepens

**Skyline Air grounds routes to eight smaller markets, and three will lose daily service until at least mid-March**

*By Staff Reporter*

Regional carrier Skyline Air announced Monday that it will cancel roughly 120 flights over the next six weeks because it does not have enough qualified pilots.

The cancellations will affect eight mid-sized and rural markets, including Cedar Falls, Marlow County, and Pine Harbor. Three of those communities will have no daily service until at least mid-March, according to a company statement.

"We deeply regret the disruption to our customers and the communities we serve," said Dana Whitfield, Skyline Air's chief operating officer. "We have exhausted every option to cover these routes safely and within federal duty-time regulations. Without enough pilots, we cannot operate the schedule we promised."

The airline said it has lost nearly 15 percent of its pilots over the past year, many of them to major carriers offering higher salaries, signing bonuses, and faster paths to international routes. Skyline now employs about 340 pilots, down from 400 last January.

Industry analysts say the problem is national. Retirements among veteran pilots, combined with a federal requirement that airline captains log 1,500 flight hours, have narrowed the pipeline of new hires. Regional airlines, which often serve as training grounds for future major-carrier pilots, have been hit hardest.

"Regionals are the farm system of the industry," said Marcus Tran, an aviation consultant. "When the big airlines hire aggressively, the regionals bleed talent. Then the small towns that depend on them lose air service, and it's very hard to get it back."

Passengers felt the effect right away. At Cedar Falls Regional Airport on Monday, traveler Priya Natarajan said her flight to a family wedding was canceled with two days' notice. "I got a text and an email, and that was it," she said. "Now I'm looking at a five-hour drive to the nearest hub."

Local officials are concerned about what happens if the service stays gone. Cedar Falls Mayor Tom Hendricks said reliable air service helps attract employers and supports local businesses. "Losing flights isn't just an inconvenience," he said. "It affects our economy."

Skyline said affected passengers will receive full refunds or be rebooked on partner airlines where possible. The company also announced a retention package that includes raises of up to 18 percent and a tuition-assistance program for aspiring pilots.

Whitfield said the airline hopes to restore full service by April but declined to guarantee a timeline.

## Public bike-share service FAQ

### 1. What is the bike-share service?
It lets you get around the city by bike. Unlock a bike at one station, ride to your destination, and return it to any available station in the network.

### 2. How do I sign up?
Use our mobile app or website. Create an account, choose a pass or membership, and add a payment method. After that, you can unlock bikes from the app.

### 3. What types of passes are available?
There are single rides, day passes, and monthly or annual memberships. Short-term passes suit visitors, and memberships suit people who ride regularly. Current prices are on our website and in the app.

### 4. How do I unlock a bike?
Open the app, find a nearby station or available bike, and scan the QR code or enter the bike number. The lock releases automatically. If it doesn't, contact customer support.

### 5. Where can I return a bike?
Return it to any official bike-share station with an open dock. Make sure the bike is locked into the dock, and wait for confirmation in the app so you aren't charged extra.

### 6. Is there a time limit for rides?
Yes. The limit depends on the pass or membership you buy, and you may pay extra fees if you go over the included ride time. You can check your ride details in the app at any time.

### 7. What if a station is full?
The app will show nearby stations with open docks. You may also get a grace period to return the bike at the next closest station.

### 8. What should I do if a bike is damaged?
Report the problem in the app as soon as you notice it, whether that's before or during your ride, and take a different bike if you need one. Reports help us keep the fleet in good condition.

### 9. Do I need to wear a helmet?
We strongly recommend a helmet for all riders. Local law may require one for certain age groups, so check the regulations where you're riding.

### 10. What happens if a bike is lost or stolen?
If a bike is lost or stolen during your rental, contact customer support right away and file a police report if one is required. You may be charged until the bike is recovered or the case is resolved.

### 11. How can I contact customer support?
You can reach support through the app, the website, or by phone. Current contact details and service hours are in the Help section.

I was raised in a family where meat was ordinary the way furniture is ordinary: always there, rarely examined. Roast chicken on Sundays, bacon on weekends, burgers in summer. No one in my house talked about the ethics of eating animals because there did not seem to be an ethical question at all. Meat was food, and food was what kept a family alive and gathered around a table. Gratitude went to the person who cooked, not to the animal that had been killed.

That changed for me slowly, through an accumulation of small discomforts. I remember seeing packaged cuts of meat in the grocery store and, for perhaps the first time, feeling the strange distance between the product and the life it came from. The clean plastic wrapping seemed designed to preserve the meat and also to spare me from thinking too much. Once I began thinking, it became difficult to stop. I realized that my appetite depended on selective attention: I liked animals in the abstract, and on my plate I preferred not to imagine them at all.

The ethical problem of eating meat, as I have come to understand it, begins with that act of avoidance. Most of us would admit that animal suffering matters at least somewhat. We recognize pain in a dog and fear in a cow. Yet our food system often treats these creatures as units of production rather than living beings with experiences of their own. If it is wrong to cause suffering unnecessarily, then industrial meat production seems especially hard to defend. The scale of confinement, mutilation, and slaughter is so vast that it resists comprehension, and perhaps that is one reason it persists. It is easier to participate in cruelty when cruelty is hidden behind branding and convenience.

At the same time, I am wary of reducing this question to a simple moral performance. Eating meat is wrapped up in culture, class, geography, and memory. For some people it is tied to tradition; for others, to survival, health, or limited access to alternatives. I do not think ethics is served by pretending all eaters stand on equal ground, free to choose from the same options. A person buying cheap meat to feed a family under financial strain is not in the same position as someone treating animal products as a luxury. Moral judgment without social context can become self-congratulation.

Still, complexity should not become an excuse for indifference. No one can live perfectly, but that is no reason not to try. I have not arrived at a pure or final answer. I eat less meat than I once did, and when I do eat it, I feel the weight of that choice more consciously. For me, the question goes beyond whether killing animals can ever be justified. I also have to ask whether I am willing to let comfort silence attention. To eat ethically, if such a thing is possible, may begin with refusing that silence, by looking steadily at what nourishes us, what it costs, and who pays the price.

A note: I'm an AI, so this is a fictional first-person essay rather than my own experience, written to sound the way such a reflection might.

## The smaller person

At thirty-four, I stood in a Lisbon bakery rehearsing a sentence. I wanted a coffee and a custard tart. I had practiced on the walk over, but when the woman behind the counter looked up, the words scattered. I pointed and said "this" twice. She smiled kindly, the way you smile at a child, and my face went hot.

Learning Portuguese showed me first how much of my adult identity rested on sounding competent. At home people consulted me. In that bakery I had the vocabulary of a toddler and the pride of a department head, and the two did not get along.

For months I was a smaller version of myself. I couldn't joke or argue, and I couldn't make the offhand observation that makes a person memorable. I had assumed my personality was solid, but it leaned heavily on grammar. What came through was patient, a little earnest, and often confused. Strangely, people liked that person. My neighbor Dona Fernanda, who was seventy and had never left Portugal, began correcting me with great ceremony. "Not *eu sou cansado*," she'd say. "*Estou* cansado. You *are* tired, but you are not *made of* tired." I have never forgotten the difference between permanent and temporary states, and I think about it in English now too.

Listening changed next. In my first language I listened lazily, already composing my reply. In Portuguese I had to catch every word as if it had been thrown to me, so I started noticing tone, gesture, and the pauses people left. I became a better listener in both languages, and I was almost embarrassed by how much I'd been missing.

Mistakes turned out to be survivable. I once told a dinner table I was "very constipated" when I meant embarrassed. (The words are false friends, and I will say no more.) The table roared, someone refilled my glass, and I felt more included than I had all week. I had spent years avoiding public failure, and it mostly made people warmer toward me.

For a long time I felt stuck. Then one afternoon I realized I had followed an entire conversation between two fast-talking taxi drivers and laughed at the right moment. Nobody gave me a certificate. I just noticed it had happened.

I still make errors daily, and I still hear the slight gentleness people use with foreigners. I used to take it for pity. Now it sounds like hospitality, offered to anyone willing to stand in front of strangers and be bad at something.

I never became fluent, exactly. What I kept from those years is the habit of pointing, saying "this," and trying again. I had stopped letting myself learn anything in front of other people, and that smaller version of me started it up again.

Listening changed next. In my first language I listened lazily, already composing my reply. In Portuguese I had to catch every word as if it had been thrown to me, so I started noticing tone, gesture, and the pauses people left. I became a better listener in both languages, and I was almost embarrassed by how much I'd been missing.

Mistakes turned out to be survivable. I once told a dinner table I was "very constipated" when I meant embarrassed. (The words are false friends, and I will say no more.) The table roared, someone refilled my glass, and I felt more included than I had all week. I had spent years avoiding public failure, and it mostly made people warmer toward me.

For a long time I felt stuck. Then one afternoon I realized I had followed an entire conversation between two fast-talking taxi drivers and laughed at the right moment. Nobody gave me a certificate. I just noticed it had happened.

I still make errors daily, and I still hear the slight gentleness people use with foreigners. I used to take it for pity. Now it sounds like hospitality, offered to anyone willing to stand in front of strangers and be bad at something.

I never became fluent, exactly. What I kept from those years is the habit of pointing, saying "this," and trying again. I had stopped letting myself learn anything in front of other people, and that smaller version of me started it up again.

# Erie Canal

The Erie Canal is a historic canal in the U.S. state of New York that connects the Hudson River at Albany with Lake Erie at Buffalo. Completed in 1825, it was the first navigable waterway linking the Atlantic seaboard to the Great Lakes, and it helped drive the growth of the U.S. economy in the nineteenth century.

## History

Proposals for a canal across upstate New York circulated in the late eighteenth century. The project gained momentum when Governor DeWitt Clinton secured state funding in 1817 after federal support failed to materialize. Critics derided it as "Clinton's Ditch." Construction began on July 4, 1817, at Rome, New York.

The canal was built largely by hand. Laborers, many of them Irish immigrants, worked with horses, oxen, and simple tools. Engineers with little formal training, such as Benjamin Wright and James Geddes, learned on the job and worked out methods for clearing forests, stumps, and swampland. The original channel was about 363 miles (584 km) long, 40 feet (12 m) wide, and 4 feet (1.2 m) deep, with 83 locks overcoming an elevation difference of roughly 565 feet (172 m).

The canal officially opened on October 26, 1825. Clinton traveled from Buffalo to New York City in a ceremonial voyage and poured Lake Erie water into the Atlantic Ocean in the "Wedding of the Waters."

## Economic and social impact

The canal cut the cost and time of moving freight. Shipping a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City fell from around $100 to roughly $10, and travel time dropped from weeks to days. Agricultural products from the Midwest flowed east, while manufactured goods and settlers moved west.

New York City surpassed rival ports such as Philadelphia and Boston to become the nation's leading commercial center. Cities along the route, including Syracuse, Rochester, Utica, and Buffalo, grew rapidly. The corridor also saw religious revivalism, the women's rights movement, and abolitionism, and some historians call western New York the "burned-over district."

## Enlargement and modern use

The canal was enlarged between 1836 and 1862. From 1905 to 1918 it was replaced by the larger New York State Barge Canal, which incorporated rivers and lakes into its route. Railroads, later highways, and the St. Lawrence Seaway reduced commercial traffic in the twentieth century.

Today the canal is used mainly for recreation, including boating, cycling, and tourism along the Erie Canalway Trail. In 2000, Congress designated the Erie Canalway National Heritage Corridor to preserve the canal's history. The New York State Canal Corporation still operates the canal.

## See also

- DeWitt Clinton
- Great Lakes
- Hudson River
- Transportation in New York

I used to think of cars as freedom. When I was younger, the center of a city seemed to begin where traffic thickened: the bright lights, the endless motion, the low growl of engines waiting at red lights. A busy street felt like proof of importance. If everyone was trying to get there, then surely that was where life was. But the older I get, the more I notice what traffic takes away from a place: conversations cut short by sirens, fumes hanging over a summer afternoon, people edging along narrow sidewalks while rows of metal sit still in the middle of the street. Now, when I think about whether cities should ban cars from their centers, I find myself leaning toward yes. I don't dislike cars. I just think city centers should belong first to people.

What changed my mind was a feeling, though there are plenty of persuasive statistics about pollution and safety. In the few places I have visited where cars were limited or absent, I felt an almost immediate release. People walked in the middle of the street without fear. Children moved unpredictably, as children do, and no one seemed angry at them for it. People lingered at outdoor tables that weren't surrounded by noise. Without cars, the city felt newly occupied by human life.

A city center is where a city presents itself to itself. Tourists form first impressions there, office workers buy lunch, elderly people try to cross the road, protests gather, and strangers become part of a crowd. If vehicles dominate that space, we have made a strange decision about our values: speed over encounter, convenience over community.

Banning cars from city centers is harder than painting over a road, and some of the objections are serious. Disabled people, delivery drivers, emergency services, and those who commute from areas with poor public transportation cannot simply be wished away. Small businesses may fear losing customers. A policy that ignores these realities will feel like punishment.

That is why a ban should be thoughtful, with exemptions, reliable public transit, better cycling infrastructure, and clear planning for deliveries and access needs. I am not declaring war on drivers. I want to ask what kind of urban life we want to encourage.

Cars are useful tools, but city centers are too important to be designed around them. If we remove cars from those spaces carefully and fairly, with alternatives in place, we may find that what seemed like sacrifice is recovery. We may get back cleaner air, quieter streets, and a stronger sense that the heart of a city is its people.

I still remember walking into my local public library as a child and sensing that I had entered a place unlike any other. It was quiet without being stiff, and it felt full of books and of possibility. I didn't have the words for what the library meant, but I understood that I was welcome there without buying anything or proving anything. That feeling has stayed with me, and it is one reason I think public libraries still matter.

Almost any piece of information is on a phone within seconds now, so it is tempting to see libraries as charming but outdated. If books can be ordered online and articles searched instantly, what is left for the library to do? Quite a lot. A public library gives people access to knowledge and treats them with dignity, and it makes a community visible.

A library is one of the few truly public spaces we have left. Most places in modern life expect us to spend money to stay. Cafés, stores, and entertainment venues all carry an unspoken price of admission. A library asks only that you respect the shared space. You can sit, read, think, learn, or rest. That openness is rare, and it says something hopeful about what a community believes people deserve.

Access to information is also less equal than we pretend. Not everyone has reliable internet, a quiet home, current technology, or the money for books and subscriptions. The public library fills those gaps with computers, internet access, job resources, research help, language learning, and educational programs. A student can study there. A job seeker can write and submit a résumé. An immigrant can find a way into a new community, and a lonely person can feel a little less alone.

Libraries also encourage slower discovery. Online, algorithms steer us toward what we already like. In a library we can wander, pulling a book from the shelf because the title surprises us or because it sits next to the one we came for. An accidental find like that can expand a life. Libraries make room for curiosity, which efficiency alone doesn't.

Public libraries also reflect a democratic ideal: knowledge should not belong only to those who can afford it. A library is a quiet argument against exclusion, saying that stories, facts, history, imagination, and opportunity should be shared.

That is why libraries still feel essential to me. A community is strongest when it invests in places where everyone is allowed to come in and grow, and the library is one of them.

# Create event

Creates a new event on a specified calendar.

Endpoint:
```
POST /v1/calendars/{calendar_id}/events
```

Authentication: Bearer token with the `calendar.events.write` scope.

## Path parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `calendar_id` | string | ID of the calendar. Use `primary` for the user's default calendar. |

## Request body

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `title` | string | Yes | Event title (max 200 characters). |
| `start` | string | Yes | Start time in ISO 8601 format, e.g. `2025-07-01T14:00:00Z`. |
| `end` | string | Yes | End time. Must be after `start`. |
| `timezone` | string | No | IANA time zone, e.g. `America/New_York`. Defaults to the calendar's time zone. |
| `description` | string | No | Event details (max 5,000 characters). |
| `location` | string | No | Physical address or meeting URL. |
| `attendees` | array | No | List of objects with an `email` field and optional `optional` boolean. |
| `reminders` | array | No | List of objects with `method` (`email` or `popup`) and `minutes_before`. |
| `recurrence` | string | No | RRULE string, e.g. `FREQ=WEEKLY;COUNT=10`. |
| `send_notifications` | boolean | No | Whether to email invitations. Default: `true`. |

## Example request

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/calendars/primary/events \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "title": "Project Kickoff",
    "start": "2025-07-01T14:00:00Z",
    "end": "2025-07-01T15:00:00Z",
    "location": "https://meet.example.com/kickoff",
    "attendees": [
      { "email": "jordan@example.com" },
      { "email": "sam@example.com", "optional": true }
    ],
    "reminders": [{ "method": "popup", "minutes_before": 10 }]
  }'
```

## Success response

Status: `201 Created`

```json
{
  "id": "evt_8f3k29x",
  "calendar_id": "primary",
  "title": "Project Kickoff",
  "start": "2025-07-01T14:00:00Z",
  "end": "2025-07-01T15:00:00Z",
  "status": "confirmed",
  "attendees": [
    { "email": "jordan@example.com", "response": "pending" },
    { "email": "sam@example.com", "optional": true, "response": "pending" }
  ],
  "created_at": "2025-06-20T09:12:44Z",
  "url": "https://calendar.example.com/events/evt_8f3k29x"
}
```

## Errors

| Status | Code | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 400 | `invalid_request` | Missing required field, malformed date, or `end` is before `start`. |
| 401 | `unauthorized` | Token is missing, invalid, or expired. |
| 403 | `insufficient_scope` | Token lacks write permission for this calendar. |
| 404 | `calendar_not_found` | The specified calendar does not exist. |
| 409 | `conflict` | An identical event already exists (when using an idempotency key). |
| 429 | `rate_limited` | Too many requests. Retry after the time in the `Retry-After` header. |

## Notes

- Include an `Idempotency-Key` header to retry requests safely without creating duplicates.
- The rate limit is 60 requests per minute per user.
- An event can have up to 200 attendees.
- For all-day events, pass dates only (e.g. `2025-07-01`) for `start` and `end`. The `end` date is exclusive.
