Friendship used to feel smaller to me, but also closer. When I was younger, a friend was someone I saw at school, someone whose house I had been to, someone whose voice I knew without checking a screen. If I wanted to tell them something, I waited until lunch, or called their home phone and hoped their parents didn't answer. That kind of friendship was slow and sometimes frustrating, but it had a certain weight. Every interaction was chosen, because you had to make time for it.

Social media changed that. At first it felt like a miracle. Friendship no longer depended on distance or schedules, and shyness mattered less. I could stay connected to people from old schools, summer programs, family trips, and later different stages of life. Someone I hadn't seen in years could still show up in my day through a photo, a joke, a birthday post, or a message sent after midnight. Friendship started to seem continuous, as if no one ever had to fully disappear.

I find that beautiful. I've seen the ordinary details of my friends' lives in a way that would have been impossible before: their new apartments, bad haircuts, pets, travel photos, engagements, breakups, and quiet victories. I've celebrated people I might otherwise have lost. Sometimes a simple reaction to a story can reopen a door, and a friendship that would have faded survives on small digital gestures. They say, "I'm still here. I still know you."

But it has also changed friendship in ways that unsettle me. It gives the feeling of intimacy without requiring the work intimacy takes. I can know what someone ate, where they vacationed, and what political opinion they posted, and still have no idea how they're actually doing. I can feel updated on a person's life without ever asking them a sincere question. Friendship starts to become passive observation, and we end up watching each other when we could be meeting.

It has also blurred what "friend" means. The number can climb into the hundreds, even thousands, and that abundance can hide a different kind of loneliness. Being visible doesn't mean being known, and getting likes doesn't comfort anyone the way a person does. Social media rewards performance, and friendship gets tangled up with presentation. Instead of sharing ourselves, we start curating ourselves, even for people who care about us. The pressure to seem happy, witty, successful, or unbothered can make honesty feel risky.

Still, I don't think social media has ruined friendship. It has shown both its strengths and its weaknesses. It helps us keep in touch and can open conversations, but it can't replace presence, and it can't guarantee depth. The friendships that matter most to me are the ones that hold up online and offline: the people I can send memes to but also call in a crisis, the people who notice when I go quiet, the people who know the version of me that exists beyond the profile.

Social media made friendship wider, faster, and more constant. What I've learned from it is that the friendships worth keeping still depend on paying attention to someone, being honest with them, and giving them your time.

Tbilisi is the capital and largest city of Georgia. It sits on the banks of the Mtkvari River in the eastern part of the country and has more than one million people. It is Georgia's political, economic, and cultural center. Because it lies at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, it has long been a hub for trade, diplomacy, and cultural exchange.

The name comes from the Georgian word "tbili," meaning "warm," after the area's natural sulfur hot springs. According to tradition, King Vakhtang I Gorgasali of Iberia founded the city in the 5th century after he found the springs while hunting. Archaeological evidence shows people living in the area earlier than that. Tbilisi became the capital of the eastern Georgian kingdom and grew into a major urban center on regional trade routes.

Persians, Arabs, Byzantines, Seljuks, Mongols, and Ottomans all fought over the city at various times. In the 19th century Russia expanded into the region, and Tbilisi became an administrative center of the Russian Empire in the Caucasus. After brief periods of independence and Soviet rule, it became the capital of independent Georgia in 1991, when the Soviet Union dissolved.

The city's architecture reflects this layered history. The Old Town has narrow streets, traditional wooden balconies, churches, mosques, and bathhouses, while later districts have neoclassical, Art Nouveau, Soviet modernist, and contemporary buildings. Landmarks include Narikala Fortress, Metekhi Church, Sameba Cathedral, Rustaveli Avenue, and the historic sulfur baths of Abanotubani.

Tbilisi is also Georgia's main center of education, arts, and science. Tbilisi State University, one of the oldest universities in the Caucasus, is based there, along with many museums, theaters, galleries, and research institutions. The Georgian National Museum, the Shota Rustaveli Theatre, and the Tbilisi Opera and Ballet Theatre are among the leading ones.

The economy rests on services, finance, tourism, transportation, and industry. Tbilisi is the country's main transportation hub, with an international airport, railway connections, and a metro system. In recent decades the city has been extensively redeveloped and modernized, though much of its historic character remains.

Archaeological evidence shows people living in the area earlier than that. Tbilisi became the capital of the eastern Georgian kingdom and grew into a major urban center on regional trade routes.

Persians, Arabs, Byzantines, Seljuks, Mongols, and Ottomans all fought over the city at various times. In the 19th century Russia expanded into the region, and Tbilisi became an administrative center of the Russian Empire in the Caucasus. After brief periods of independence and Soviet rule, it became the capital of independent Georgia in 1991, when the Soviet Union dissolved.

The city's architecture reflects this layered history. The Old Town has narrow streets, traditional wooden balconies, churches, mosques, and bathhouses, while later districts have neoclassical, Art Nouveau, Soviet modernist, and contemporary buildings. Landmarks include Narikala Fortress, Metekhi Church, Sameba Cathedral, Rustaveli Avenue, and the historic sulfur baths of Abanotubani.

Tbilisi is also Georgia's main center of education, arts, and science. Tbilisi State University, one of the oldest universities in the Caucasus, is based there, along with many museums, theaters, galleries, and research institutions. The Georgian National Museum, the Shota Rustaveli Theatre, and the Tbilisi Opera and Ballet Theatre are among the leading ones.

The economy rests on services, finance, tourism, transportation, and industry. Tbilisi is the country's main transportation hub, with an international airport, railway connections, and a metro system. In recent decades the city has been extensively redeveloped and modernized, though much of its historic character remains.

# Library of Alexandria

The Library of Alexandria was one of the largest libraries of the ancient world, located in Alexandria, Egypt. Founded in the early 3rd century BCE under the Ptolemaic dynasty, it formed part of a research institution known as the Mouseion (Museum), dedicated to the Muses. The library became a symbol of ancient learning and, in popular culture, of knowledge lost to destruction.

## History

The library was probably established during the reign of Ptolemy I Soter (r. 305-282 BCE) or his son Ptolemy II Philadelphus (r. 284-246 BCE). Demetrius of Phalerum, an Athenian exile, is traditionally credited with advising on its creation, though modern scholars debate his role. The Ptolemies sought to gather texts from across the known world. According to ancient sources, ships entering Alexandria's harbor were searched for books, which were copied and sometimes kept, with the owners receiving the copies instead.

## Collection and scholarship

Estimates of the library's holdings vary widely, with ancient writers citing figures from 40,000 to 700,000 scrolls. These numbers are generally considered unreliable. The collection included works of literature, history, mathematics, medicine, and philosophy, largely in Greek but also in translation from other languages. According to tradition, the Hebrew scriptures were translated into Greek there, producing the Septuagint.

Many prominent scholars worked there. Euclid is associated with Alexandria and produced his *Elements* there. Eratosthenes, who served as librarian, calculated the Earth's circumference. Aristarchus of Samothrace edited Homeric texts, and Callimachus compiled the *Pinakes*, an early catalog of the collection. Herophilus and Erasistratus advanced the study of anatomy in the city.

## Decline and destruction

The library declined over several centuries. Julius Caesar's fire in 48 BCE, set during his conflict in Alexandria, damaged part of the city and may have destroyed some books, though its extent is uncertain. Under Roman rule, funding and royal patronage declined. Aurelian's campaign in the 270s CE devastated the district containing the Mouseion. The Serapeum, a "daughter library," was destroyed in 391 CE under Bishop Theophilus. Most historians regard the story that the Arab conqueror Amr ibn al-As burned the library in 642 CE as a later legend.

## Modern legacy

In 2002, Egypt opened the Bibliotheca Alexandrina near the ancient site, a modern library and cultural center meant to revive the original institution.

## See also

- Ptolemaic Kingdom
- Library of Pergamum
- Septuagint

# Plugin system documentation

## Overview

The editor's plugin system lets you extend functionality without modifying the core application. Plugins are written in JavaScript and run in an isolated sandbox, communicating with the editor through a controlled API.

## Installing plugins

Place plugin folders in your user plugin directory:

- Windows: `%APPDATA%\Editor\plugins`
- macOS/Linux: `~/.config/editor/plugins`

Alternatively, open the command palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P`) and run **Plugins: Install from Registry**. Restart the editor or run **Plugins: Reload All** to activate new plugins.

## Plugin structure

Each plugin requires a folder containing at least two files:

```
my-plugin/
├── manifest.json
└── index.js
```

### manifest.json

The manifest describes your plugin:

```json
{
  "name": "word-counter",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "index.js",
  "permissions": ["editor.read", "ui.statusbar"],
  "activationEvents": ["onStartup"]
}
```

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `name` | Unique identifier, lowercase with hyphens |
| `version` | Semantic version string |
| `main` | Entry point file |
| `permissions` | APIs the plugin may access |
| `activationEvents` | When the plugin loads |

## Writing a plugin

Your entry file must export an `activate` function. Export `deactivate` if cleanup is needed.

```javascript
exports.activate = function (editor) {
  const item = editor.ui.createStatusItem();

  editor.on("textChanged", () => {
    const text = editor.document.getText();
    item.setText(`Words: ${text.split(/\s+/).length}`);
  });
};

exports.deactivate = function () {
  // Release resources here
};
```

## Core API

- `editor.document`: Read and modify the active file (`getText()`, `insert()`, `replace()`)
- `editor.commands`: Register commands with `registerCommand(id, handler)`
- `editor.ui`: Create status items, menus, and panels
- `editor.on(event, callback)`: Subscribe to events such as `textChanged`, `fileSaved`, and `selectionChanged`
- `editor.settings`: Read user configuration values

## Permissions

Plugins can only use APIs declared in their manifest. Common permissions include:

- `editor.read`: Read document contents
- `editor.write`: Modify documents
- `ui.statusbar`: Add status bar items
- `fs.read`: Read files in the workspace
- `network`: Make external requests

The editor prompts users to approve permissions on first install.

## Debugging

Open **Help → Toggle Plugin Console** to view logs from `console.log` and uncaught errors. Use **Plugins: Reload All** after making changes to see updates immediately.

## Best practices

1. Request only the permissions you need.
2. Use specific activation events instead of `onStartup` to keep launch times fast.
3. Dispose of event listeners in `deactivate`.
4. Avoid blocking operations; use asynchronous calls for file and network access.

# Design Document: API Caching Layer

## Overview

This document proposes adding a distributed caching layer to our web API to reduce database load, lower response latency, and improve scalability under peak traffic.

## Problem Statement

Our API currently queries the primary PostgreSQL database for every request. Profiling shows that 80% of traffic hits read-only endpoints (product catalogs, user profiles, configuration data), many returning identical results across requests. During peak hours, p95 latency exceeds 800ms and database CPU regularly reaches 85%.

## Goals

- Reduce p95 latency on read endpoints to under 150ms
- Cut database read load by at least 60%
- Keep staleness under 60 seconds for most resources
- Avoid changes to client-facing API contracts

## Non-Goals

- Caching authenticated write operations
- Replacing the database as the source of truth

## Proposed Solution

Introduce Redis as a cache-aside layer between the API servers and the database.

Read path: The API checks Redis using a deterministic key (e.g., `product:v1:{id}`). On a hit, it returns the cached value. On a miss, it queries the database, stores the result with a TTL, and returns it.

Write path: Upon update or deletion, the API invalidates the relevant keys. List and search results use short TTLs (30 seconds) instead of explicit invalidation, since tracking dependencies is error-prone.

Key design: Version prefixes allow bulk invalidation after schema changes. Per-user data includes the user ID in the key to prevent leakage.

TTL strategy:

| Resource | TTL |
|---|---|
| Configuration | 10 min |
| Product details | 5 min (plus invalidation) |
| Lists/search | 30 sec |

## Risks and Mitigations

- Stampedes: When popular keys expire, many requests may hit the database simultaneously. We will use request coalescing and add random jitter (±10%) to TTLs.
- Stale data: Explicit invalidation on writes plus conservative TTLs limit exposure.
- Redis outage: The API will fall back to the database with a circuit breaker. Performance will degrade, but requests will still succeed.
- Memory growth: Enforce `allkeys-lru` eviction and monitor memory usage.

## Rollout Plan

1. Deploy a managed Redis cluster with replication
2. Implement caching behind a feature flag, starting with configuration endpoints
3. Roll out to 10%, then 50%, then 100% of traffic per endpoint
4. Monitor hit rate, latency, and error rates at each stage

## Success Metrics

Cache hit rate above 75%, p95 latency under 150ms, and database CPU below 50% at peak.

## Open Questions

- Should we add an in-process L1 cache for extremely hot keys?
- Is a CDN appropriate for public, unauthenticated endpoints?

# Voyager 1

Voyager 1 is a space probe launched by NASA on September 5, 1977, as part of the Voyager program to study the outer Solar System and interstellar space. It was launched sixteen days after its twin, Voyager 2, and is the most distant human-made object from Earth, traveling at roughly 17 kilometers per second (about 61,000 km/h) relative to the Sun.

## Mission background

The Voyager program took advantage of a rare alignment of the outer planets that occurs about once every 175 years, which let spacecraft use gravity assists to travel between multiple planets. The probes were built by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) and originally funded for a four-year mission to Jupiter and Saturn.

## Spacecraft design

Voyager 1 had a mass of about 825 kilograms at launch and carries a 3.7-meter high-gain antenna for communication with the Deep Space Network. Three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) supply power by converting heat from decaying plutonium-238 into electricity. Their output declines by several watts each year, so engineers have had to switch off nonessential instruments and heaters over time. The spacecraft also carries the Golden Record, a gold-plated phonograph record containing sounds, images, and music representing life and culture on Earth.

## Planetary encounters

Voyager 1 made its closest approach to Jupiter on March 5, 1979, and revealed active volcanism on the moon Io, the first volcanic activity observed beyond Earth. It reached Saturn on November 12, 1980, and returned detailed images of the planet's rings and of its largest moon, Titan, whose thick atmosphere was studied closely. The Titan flyby bent the probe's trajectory out of the ecliptic plane, which ended its planetary tour. In 1990, it captured the "Family Portrait" of the Solar System, including the image of Earth known as the *Pale Blue Dot*.

## Interstellar mission

On August 25, 2012, Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the boundary where the Sun's solar wind gives way to the interstellar medium, and became the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. Its plasma wave instrument measured a sharp rise in plasma density that confirmed the crossing.

In November 2023, the probe began sending unintelligible data because of a fault in one of its onboard computers. Engineers at JPL traced the fault to a corrupted memory chip in the flight data subsystem and, in 2024, restored communication by relocating the affected code. The spacecraft was then more than 24 billion kilometers away.

## Future

Voyager 1 continues to transmit data on magnetic fields, cosmic rays, and plasma. Mission planners expect the RTGs to power at least one instrument into the mid-2020s, possibly later. The probe will keep drifting through the Milky Way and will pass within about 1.6 light-years of the star Gliese 445 in roughly 40,000 years.

## See also

- Voyager 2
- Voyager program
- Pioneer 10
- Golden Record

# The Last Free Room

When I was nine, my family moved to a new town in the middle of winter, and for weeks I knew no one. My mother worked two jobs. My father was still back in our old city, finishing out a lease. The apartment was small and quiet, and the afternoons were long. One day I followed a stranger's dog down the street and ended up in front of the public library.

It was the only place in town that wanted nothing from me. I didn't see that then. I see it now, having learned how rare it is. Almost everywhere else, taking up space means buying something: coffee shops want you to order a latte, and malls want you to leave with a receipt. Even parks have their rules and hours. The library lets you come in, sit down, and stay as long as you like. I think it may be the last free room in American life, and we undervalue it because it asks so little.

People say libraries are obsolete because everything is online anyway. That ignores how much a library does. It lends books, and a shared shelf where one copy of a novel can pass through fifty hands is a good thing in itself. But spend an afternoon in one and you'll see plenty more. A man in a worn jacket fills out a job application on a public computer while a librarian patiently helps him attach his résumé. A teenager does her homework because her home has no internet. A toddler learns to sit through a story. Someone gets help with tax forms, someone else is learning English, and someone is simply warm for a few hours, out of the cold. The library treats all of them as citizens, and none of them has to pay to be there.

The library also starts from the premise that knowledge shouldn't depend on your ability to pay for it. The idea is old, but it matters more now, when so much information sits behind paywalls and algorithms decide what we see. A library's shelves are curated by people trained to help you find what's true, and they have no stake in keeping you scrolling. A librarian will answer your question without tracking you or selling your data, and without pointing you toward an ad.

That winter I worked through the children's section, then the adult one, then whatever a kind librarian slid across the desk with a raised eyebrow and a "Try this." I read about places I'd never see and lives nothing like mine. Somewhere along the way I stopped feeling like the new kid and started feeling like part of something larger.

I still carry a library card, and it's one of my most prized possessions. It stands for a bargain we made with one another: we pool our resources so that everyone, whatever their circumstances, can have access to the world. I think we should keep it.

European museum returns 27 looted artifacts to Nigeria

A major European museum has returned 27 looted artifacts to Nigeria.

At a ceremony on Tuesday, the museum handed the objects over to Nigerian officials. They include ceremonial sculptures, carved ivory pieces, and bronze plaques taken during a 19th-century military expedition. The artifacts had been housed in the museum's African collections for more than a century. They are expected to go on display in Lagos after conservation work is completed.

Museum director Elise Hartmann called the return "a moral responsibility and an institutional reckoning."

"These objects were acquired in circumstances that were deeply unjust," Hartmann said. "They are not simply works of art; they are part of a living cultural heritage. Returning them is the right thing to do."

The return follows years of pressure from Nigerian officials, scholars, and activists, who have argued that artifacts seized during colonial campaigns should go back to the communities they were taken from. Provenance research by the museum found that the objects were removed during a British punitive raid in 1897 and later sold through European art markets before entering the museum's collection.

Nigeria's Minister of Culture, Amina Bello, welcomed the return, calling it "an important act of justice, dignity, and historical acknowledgment."

"For generations, these treasures were admired abroad while the people to whom they belong were denied access to them," Bello said. "Their return does not erase the past, but it helps us confront it honestly and begin to repair the damage."

Many museums in Europe and North America are reexamining items acquired during the colonial period. In recent years, several have announced the return of bronzes, sacred objects, and human remains after evidence showed they had been taken through violence, coercion, or theft.

The issue is still contested. Some critics argue that museums serve a global public and should keep major collections while sharing them through loans and partnerships. Others say full repatriation is necessary to correct long-standing injustices and restore cultural sovereignty.

Art historian Daniel Okoye said the return could encourage similar actions elsewhere. "This is not just about one museum or one set of objects," he said. "It signals a growing recognition that possession without consent cannot be justified indefinitely."

The museum said it plans to continue reviewing the provenance of hundreds of items in its collection and is in discussions with other countries about possible returns.

The issue is still contested. Some critics argue that museums serve a global public and should keep major collections while sharing them through loans and partnerships. Others say full repatriation is necessary to correct long-standing injustices and restore cultural sovereignty.

Art historian Daniel Okoye said the return could encourage similar actions elsewhere. "This is not just about one museum or one set of objects," he said. "It signals a growing recognition that possession without consent cannot be justified indefinitely."

The museum said it plans to continue reviewing the provenance of hundreds of items in its collection and is in discussions with other countries about possible returns.

Antikythera mechanism

The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient Greek hand-powered mechanical device, generally considered the earliest known analog computer. It calculated and displayed astronomical phenomena, including the positions of the Sun and Moon, lunar phases, and eclipse cycles, and possibly the motions of some planets. It is usually dated to the late 2nd or early 1st century BCE.

It was discovered in 1901 among the remains of a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera, between Crete and the Peloponnese. It came up as a set of heavily corroded bronze fragments and got little attention at first. Only decades later did researchers find finely cut gears inside the fragments. X-ray computed tomography and other modern imaging have since revealed much of its internal structure and inscriptions.

The device sat in a wooden case roughly the size of a shoebox. The front face had circular dials with pointers, probably showing the zodiac and the Egyptian calendar. A hand crank probably drove a system of more than 30 bronze gears, which turned rotation into the ratios of celestial cycles. To model the Moon's irregular motion, a pin-and-slot arrangement varied the lunar speed in line with Greek astronomical theory.

The back held spiral dials for longer cycles. One showed the Metonic cycle of 19 years, which reconciles lunar months with the solar year. Another tracked the Saros cycle, used to predict eclipses. A subsidiary dial appears to have marked the Exeligmos, a longer eclipse cycle that improves prediction accuracy. Inscriptions on the device worked as an operating manual, explaining the dials and displays.

The gearing is more precise than scholars once thought Hellenistic craftsmen could achieve, which points to an established tradition of instrument-making, though no other surviving device of comparable complexity from antiquity is known. Scholars have linked it to Greek scientific traditions associated with Hipparchus, Posidonius, and Archimedes, but its exact origin and maker remain uncertain.

It shows that Greek craftsmen and astronomers could build advanced mathematical knowledge into a working mechanism.

The Street That Learned to Breathe

The first time I stood in a city center with no cars, the sounds caught my attention before the absence did: a busker's out-of-tune accordion, a toddler shrieking with joy at a pigeon, two old men arguing over chess. It took me a full minute to work out what was missing, the low, constant growl I had always mistaken for silence.

That was in a mid-sized European city, on a trip I'd taken mostly to escape my own. At home, I drive everywhere. I'm not proud of it, but I won't pretend otherwise. My downtown is a place I endure: circling for parking, paying too much for it, then walking half a mile past gray garages. So when people propose banning cars from city centers, my first instinct is defensive. What about my groceries? What about my mother, who can't walk far? What about the plumber, the ambulance, the delivery driver?

Those questions deserve real answers, and the best car-free centers have them. Ambulances and fire trucks get through. Residents with disabilities get permits and drop-off zones. Deliveries happen in early-morning windows. A well-run ban works like a filter. It says the busiest, most valuable square mile of a city shouldn't be organized around the least efficient way to move people through it.

And it is inefficient. A single lane of car traffic moves maybe 2,000 people an hour. The same width given to a tram or to pedestrians moves many times that. We devote staggering amounts of prime real estate to storing empty vehicles, then wonder why rents are high and public space is scarce.

Still, I don't think the answer is a clean yes. I've seen bans imposed on cities that offered nothing in return: no reliable buses and no safe bike lanes. In those places, a ban doesn't create a lively plaza. It punishes the shift worker who commutes from the outskirts at midnight, when the trains have stopped. Cities that ban first and build later are running an experiment on their poorest residents.

So my view is conditional. Cities should move toward car-free centers, and they should earn it by building the alternatives first, or at least at the same time. Make the train faster than the drive. Make the bike lane feel safe to an eleven-year-old. Then close the street, and people will barely argue.

What changed my mind was watching that European square at dusk, when the chess players packed up and families took their place, children weaving between café tables without a parent's hand clamped to their shoulder. Nobody was in a hurry or in danger, and the whole square felt like a living room.

I still drive at home. But I've started parking at the edge of downtown and walking in. The first few times, it felt like a loss. Now it feels like practice for a city where the center belongs to the people in it.

# Artemisia Gentileschi

Artemisia Gentileschi (born 8 July 1593, died c. 1656) was an Italian Baroque painter and one of the leading artists of her generation. Working in the tradition of Caravaggio, she painted dramatic, naturalistic compositions, often showing heroic women from myth, scripture, and history. She was the first woman admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno in Florence.

## Early life

Artemisia was born in Rome, the eldest child of the painter Orazio Gentileschi and Prudentia Montone. Her mother died when Artemisia was about twelve. She trained in her father's workshop, where she learned drawing, color mixing, and painting techniques. Women were barred from formal academies, so her education took place almost entirely in the studio. Her earliest signed work, *Susanna and the Elders* (1610), was painted when she was seventeen and already shows great skill.

## Trial of Agostino Tassi

In 1611, Artemisia was raped by Agostino Tassi, a painter and colleague of her father who had been hired to teach her perspective. Orazio brought charges in 1612, and a seven-month trial followed. Artemisia was reportedly examined under torture with thumbscrews to verify her testimony. Tassi was convicted, but his sentence of exile from Rome was not enforced for long. The surviving trial transcripts are one of the few records of a woman's testimony from this period.

## Career

Shortly after the trial, Artemisia married the Florentine artist Pierantonio Stiattesi and moved to Florence. She was successful there, winning the patronage of Cosimo II de' Medici and becoming friends with Galileo Galilei. In 1616 she became a member of the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno. Her works from this period include *Judith Slaying Holofernes* (c. 1614 to 1620) and *Self-Portrait as a Lute Player*.

Debts and financial difficulties led her to return to Rome in the 1620s, and she later worked in Venice and Naples. In 1638 she joined her father at the court of Charles I in England, and after Orazio's death in 1639 she completed some of his commissions. She spent much of her later career in Naples, where she collaborated with other painters and received prominent commissions.

## Style and themes

Gentileschi's paintings are marked by strong chiaroscuro, vivid color, and emotional intensity. She often painted Judith, Susanna, Esther, Bathsheba, and Cleopatra. Her heroines are physically strong and psychologically complex, unlike the more passive women common in the work of her male contemporaries.

## Legacy

After her death, Gentileschi was largely overlooked for centuries. In the 20th century, art historians, notably feminist scholars, rediscovered her work and reassessed her significance. Her life and art have since inspired books, plays, and films, and major exhibitions, including one at the National Gallery, London, in 2020, have raised her standing as a Baroque master.

# Migration guide: config format v1 to v2

Version 2 of the configuration format groups settings into sections, enforces value types, and renames several fields. This guide lists the changes and shows how to update existing v1 files.

## Summary of breaking changes

1. Top-level keys are now grouped into sections.
2. Several field names have changed.
3. Booleans and numbers must be native YAML/JSON types, not strings.
4. Environment-specific overrides moved to a dedicated `environments` block.
5. Deprecated v1 fields are no longer supported.

## Key changes

### 1. Top-level structure

In v1, most settings lived at the root level. In v2 they are grouped under four keys:

- `server`
- `logging`
- `auth`
- `environments`

### 2. Renamed fields

Common renames:

- `host` → `server.host`
- `port` → `server.port`
- `logLevel` → `logging.level`
- `logFile` → `logging.file`
- `enableAuth` → `auth.enabled`

### 3. Strict value types

v1 often accepted strings such as `"true"` or `"8080"`. v2 requires native types:

- `"true"` → `true`
- `"8080"` → `8080`

### 4. Environment overrides

v1 used flattened keys such as `dev_host` or `prod_port`. In v2 these go under `environments`:

```yaml
environments:
  dev:
    server:
      host: ...
  prod:
    server:
      port: ...
```

## Example migration

### v1

```yaml
host: "localhost"
port: "8080"
logLevel: "debug"
logFile: "/var/log/app.log"
enableAuth: "true"
dev_host: "dev.local"
prod_host: "prod.example.com"
```

### v2

```yaml
server:
  host: localhost
  port: 8080

logging:
  level: debug
  file: /var/log/app.log

auth:
  enabled: true

environments:
  dev:
    server:
      host: dev.local
  prod:
    server:
      host: prod.example.com
```

## Removed fields

These v1 fields are no longer supported in v2:

- `timeoutMs`: replaced by `server.timeout`, which is in seconds
- `authModeLegacy`: removed; use `auth.provider`
- `debug`: replaced by `logging.level: debug`

## Migration tips

- Validate the file against the v2 schema before deployment.
- Update any automation scripts that read the old field names.
- Quoted booleans and numbers now fail validation, so check for them.
- Migrate in a staging environment first, one step at a time.

## Checklist

- [ ] Nest root settings under the correct sections
- [ ] Rename deprecated keys
- [ ] Convert stringified booleans and numbers to native types
- [ ] Move environment-specific values into `environments`
- [ ] Remove unsupported legacy fields

# photodate

Rename your photos by the date they were taken. `photodate` reads EXIF metadata and renames files to a consistent, sortable format like `2024-07-14_15-32-08.jpg`.

## Features

- Reads the original capture date from EXIF data
- Falls back to the file's modified time when EXIF is missing
- Customizable filename templates
- Dry-run mode to preview changes
- Automatic handling of duplicate timestamps
- Undo support for the most recent run
- Works on JPEG, HEIC, PNG, TIFF, and common RAW formats

## Installation

With pip:

```bash
pip install photodate
```

Or from source:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/example/photodate.git
cd photodate
pip install .
```

Requires Python 3.9 or newer.

## Usage

```bash
photodate [OPTIONS] PATH...
```

`PATH` can be one or more files or directories.

### Quick start

Preview what would change:

```bash
photodate --dry-run ~/Pictures/vacation
```

Rename for real:

```bash
photodate ~/Pictures/vacation
```

Include subfolders:

```bash
photodate --recursive ~/Pictures
```

## Options

| Option | Description |
|---|---|
| `-n`, `--dry-run` | Show planned renames without changing anything |
| `-r`, `--recursive` | Process directories recursively |
| `-f`, `--format TEMPLATE` | Filename template (default: `%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S`) |
| `--fallback [mtime\|skip]` | What to do when EXIF is missing (default: `mtime`) |
| `--prefix TEXT` | Add a prefix to every filename |
| `--lowercase-ext` | Convert file extensions to lowercase |
| `--undo` | Revert the last run |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | Print every rename |

## Templates

Templates use standard `strftime` codes:

```bash
photodate --format "%Y/%m/IMG_%Y%m%d_%H%M%S" photos/
```

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `%Y` | Four-digit year |
| `%m` | Month (01 to 12) |
| `%d` | Day of month |
| `%H` `%M` `%S` | Hour, minute, second |

## Duplicate timestamps

Burst shots often share the same timestamp. When names collide, `photodate` appends a counter:

```
2024-07-14_15-32-08.jpg
2024-07-14_15-32-08_2.jpg
2024-07-14_15-32-08_3.jpg
```

Existing files are never overwritten.

## Undo

Each run writes a log to `~/.photodate/last_run.json`. To revert:

```bash
photodate --undo
```

Only the most recent run can be undone.

## Contributing

Bug reports and pull requests are welcome. Please run `pytest` before submitting changes.

## License

MIT

# Museum returns 27 looted artifacts to Nigeria

**Benin bronzes and ceremonial objects will go on display in Benin City after more than a century abroad**

*Hartwell, England:* A regional museum in northern England formally returned 27 artifacts to Nigeria on Tuesday. The objects were taken during a colonial-era military expedition in 1897, and the handover ended a decade of negotiations.

The Hartwell Museum of World Cultures transferred legal ownership of the collection to Nigeria's National Commission for Museums and Monuments at a ceremony attended by diplomats, museum staff, and members of the Edo diaspora community. The items include brass plaques, carved ivory pieces, and a ceremonial staff that once belonged to the royal court of the Kingdom of Benin.

"These are not simply objects," said Dr. Amara Okonkwo, the Nigerian delegation's lead representative. "They are records of our history, our artistry, and our identity. For generations, our communities have studied these works through photographs in foreign books. Today, that changes."

British forces attacked Benin City in 1897 and removed thousands of items from the royal palace. Many were sold at auction or passed to private collectors and institutions across Europe and North America. The museum acquired its pieces in 1934 through a bequest from the family of a former naval officer.

Museum director Helen Marsh said the decision followed extensive provenance research, which confirmed the objects' origins beyond reasonable doubt. "We had to ask ourselves what responsibility we have when we know how an object came to us," Marsh said. "The answer, ultimately, was clear. Holding onto them was no longer defensible."

Pressure on Western institutions to address colonial-era acquisitions is growing. In recent years, museums in Germany, the United States, and Scotland have returned portions of their Benin collections, while the British Museum continues to face calls to return its much larger holdings.

Some curators argue that universal museums let global audiences encounter diverse cultures. Others worry about conservation capacity, though supporters of restitution note that Nigeria is building the Edo Museum of West African Art, designed by architect David Adjaye, to house returned works.

Chidi Eze, a London-based university student of Edo descent, attended the ceremony. "My grandmother used to tell me stories about the palace and the bronzes," he said. "I never thought I would see any of this come home in my lifetime."

The artifacts will be flown to Lagos next week and then taken to Benin City, where they are expected to go on public display by early next year.

"We had to ask ourselves what responsibility we have when we know how an object came to us," Marsh said. "The answer, ultimately, was clear. Holding onto them was no longer defensible."

Pressure on Western institutions to address colonial-era acquisitions is growing. In recent years, museums in Germany, the United States, and Scotland have returned portions of their Benin collections, while the British Museum continues to face calls to return its much larger holdings.

Some curators argue that universal museums let global audiences encounter diverse cultures. Others worry about conservation capacity, though supporters of restitution note that Nigeria is building the Edo Museum of West African Art, designed by architect David Adjaye, to house returned works.

Chidi Eze, a London-based university student of Edo descent, attended the ceremony. "My grandmother used to tell me stories about the palace and the bronzes," he said. "I never thought I would see any of this come home in my lifetime."

The artifacts will be flown to Lagos next week and then taken to Benin City, where they are expected to go on public display by early next year.

Boredom has an unfair reputation. We treat it as a minor curse, to be avoided as urgently as hunger or loneliness. A boring class or a boring afternoon feels like a failure of design, proof that life is not entertaining us as it should. For a long time I agreed. If I was waiting in line, sitting on a bus, or staring at the ceiling with nothing to do, I reached for my phone almost automatically. I treated every empty space in the day as a problem to solve. Only later did I notice that some of those spaces were not empty at all. They gave me room.

As a child, I met boredom at its purest on summer afternoons. The heat was too heavy for running outside, the television offered nothing, and my friends were away. At first those hours felt unbearable. I paced from room to room, telling anyone who would listen that there was "nothing to do." But once the complaining wore itself out, I usually started building strange worlds from ordinary things. Blankets became forts, notebooks became newspapers for imaginary cities, and a box of mismatched buttons became treasure. I had to get through the boredom before my imagination would start working.

That pattern did not disappear when I grew up. It just got harder to see. Adults have endless ways out of boredom, many of them glowing in the palm of the hand. The moment a task turns repetitive or a silence stretches, a distraction is there. But constant stimulation leaves me feeling oddly thin, as though my attention has broken into so many pieces that none of them can settle. Boredom tends to gather me back together. It slows time enough for thoughts I have been avoiding, or have been too busy to hear, to come to the surface.

Some of my clearest ideas have arrived in dull moments: folding laundry, walking a familiar route, sitting through the first uneventful minutes of a delayed train. My mind wanders in those moments, and the wandering is often where reflection begins. Without urgency, my attention gets less efficient but roomier, and memory, curiosity, and old discomfort get a turn to speak. Without those moments, I suspect I would know less about what I think.

Boredom also has a moral side. Being bored means admitting that not every moment exists for our amusement, and that the world does not owe us constant novelty. Sitting still in a waiting room, listening through a quiet pause, or letting an afternoon unfold without demanding instant gratification is a way of practicing patience, and it humbles me a little. A meaningful life is made of thrilling scenes, but also of ordinary stretches that ask for endurance and some invention.

I still dislike boredom sometimes, and I still reach for distraction more often than I mean to. But I no longer see it as a void to fill as quickly as possible. I see it as an interval I need, one in which quieter thoughts have a chance to show up. These days it may be one of the few places left where I can hear myself think.

# Contributing Guide

Thanks for your interest in contributing to our open-source documentation website. We welcome fixes for typos, clearer explanations, new content, and suggestions for restructuring.

## Ways to contribute

You can:

- Fix spelling, grammar, or formatting
- Clarify existing explanations
- Add examples, tutorials, or reference material
- Report outdated or incorrect information
- Improve accessibility and readability
- Suggest better navigation or organization

If you are unsure whether your idea fits, open an issue first.

## Before you start

- Read the existing documentation to get a feel for its style and structure.
- Search open issues and pull requests so you don't duplicate work.
- Check for an existing discussion about the change you want to make.

For larger changes, please open an issue before writing content so we can agree on the approach and save you rework.

## Getting started

1. Fork the repository.
2. Create a new branch for your changes.
3. Make your edits.
4. Preview the site locally if you can.
5. Commit with a clear message.
6. Open a pull request.

Use descriptive branch names such as `fix-installation-typo` or `add-api-auth-guide`.

## Writing guidelines

- Write in clear, direct language and avoid unnecessary jargon.
- Use short paragraphs and descriptive headings.
- Prefer examples to abstract explanations.
- Keep terminology consistent across pages.
- Link to related pages where helpful.

Make sure technical examples are accurate and easy to follow. If you include a command or code snippet, test it whenever possible.

## Style and formatting

Follow the project's conventions for:

- Markdown structure and heading levels
- Code block formatting with language tags
- File naming
- Internal linking

If the repository has linting or formatting tools, run them before you submit your pull request.

## Pull request expectations

A good pull request:

- Explains what changed and why
- Stays focused on a single topic when possible
- Includes screenshots or previews for visual changes

Reviews are a normal part of the process, so expect feedback. Collaboration improves the result.

## Reporting issues

If you find a problem but don't want to submit a fix, open an issue. Include:

- A clear title
- A link to the affected page
- A description of the problem
- A suggestion, if you have one

## Code of conduct

Please be respectful and constructive in all interactions. We want the project to be welcoming to contributors of every experience level.

When people talk about the decline of letter writing, they usually start with nostalgia: the envelopes, the stamps, the pleasure of recognizing a familiar hand before reading a word. All of that is real. But giving up letters costs more than a charming old ritual. It costs us a way of thinking and feeling, and a way of being present to one another.

A letter asks something different of us than a text or an email. It asks us to sit still long enough to find out what we want to say. Most modern communication is built for speed. We reply quickly, revise where no one can see, send half-thoughts, and fill silence before it can deepen. A letter moves at the pace of reflection. Because it takes time to write, seal, send, and receive, it encourages a more deliberate honesty. You rarely spend a letter on what you had for lunch or a passing irritation. You gather yourself and shape experience into language, and often you come to understand your own mind better.

I think this is one of the quietest losses: a private workshop for the self. A letter sits between conversation and diary. It is personal but directed outward, written to a particular person rather than into the void, and that audience matters. We become slightly better versions of ourselves in letters, more thoughtful, more generous, more willing to explain what we mean. Writing to someone we love can refine our character as well as our words.

Letters also preserve feeling in a way instant messages rarely do. A text can say "I miss you," but a letter carries the physical evidence of having been made by someone's hands. The pressure of the pen, the slant of the lines, the crossings-out, the margin added as an afterthought: these are traces of a living moment. A letter is language, but it is also an object. It travels through weather and distance. It can be folded into a drawer, reopened years later, and bring back a lost version of a person. Holding an old letter, you meet what someone felt and how they moved through time.

Without letters we also lose some patience with absence. Letters teach us to wait, and the waiting is not empty. It deepens affection and gives longing room to ripen into attention. Now that we can reach anyone instantly, we expect access instead of presence, and we confuse constant contact with closeness. Closeness doesn't always grow from frequency. Sometimes it grows from concentration, from choosing words carefully, from speaking across silence rather than erasing it.

I don't think we have to reject new forms of communication to mourn what letters gave us. Texts are useful, emails efficient, calls immediate. But letters offered something these forms seldom do: a durable record of thought shaped by time and care. They are one of the few ways of communicating that ask us to slow down enough to mean what we say.

# Migrating configuration files from v1 to v2

This guide covers the changes between v1 and v2 of the configuration format and how to update your files. Examples use YAML.

## Summary of changes

| Area | v1 | v2 |
|---|---|---|
| Version field | Optional | Required (`version: 2`) |
| Server settings | Flat keys | Nested under `server` |
| Timeouts | Integers (seconds) | Duration strings (`"30s"`) |
| Environment variables | `$VAR` | `${VAR}` or `${VAR:-default}` |
| Booleans | `yes`/`no` accepted | `true`/`false` only |
| `log_file` | Supported | Removed; use `logging.output` |

## Step 1: Add the version field

Add this at the top of every file. v2 parsers reject files without it.

```yaml
version: 2
```

## Step 2: Nest server settings

The flat `host`, `port`, and `timeout` keys now live under `server`.

v1:
```yaml
host: 0.0.0.0
port: 8080
timeout: 30
```

v2:
```yaml
server:
  host: 0.0.0.0
  port: 8080
  timeout: "30s"
```

## Step 3: Convert timeouts to durations

All time values must be strings with a unit: `ms`, `s`, `m`, or `h`. Bare integers now raise a validation error because the old implicit unit (seconds) caused confusion.

## Step 4: Update environment variable syntax

Change `$DB_PASSWORD` to `${DB_PASSWORD}`. You can now supply fallbacks:

```yaml
database:
  password: ${DB_PASSWORD:-changeme}
```

Literal dollar signs must be escaped as `$$`.

## Step 5: Replace deprecated options

`log_file` is removed. Use the `logging` block instead:

v1:
```yaml
log_file: /var/log/app.log
```

v2:
```yaml
logging:
  output: /var/log/app.log
  level: info
```

## Step 6: Fix boolean values

Replace `yes`, `no`, `on`, and `off` with `true` or `false`. v2 follows YAML 1.2, which no longer treats the older forms as booleans.

## Automated migration

A converter handles most of these changes:

```bash
config-tool migrate --from 1 --to 2 config.yaml -o config.v2.yaml
```

Review the output before deploying. The tool cannot infer the right `logging.level`, so it defaults to `info`.

## Validating the result

```bash
config-tool validate config.v2.yaml
```

Fix any reported errors, which include line numbers.

## Rollback

Keep your v1 files until v2 has run successfully in production. v1 files remain readable by v1-compatible releases, but v2 files are not backward compatible.

## Common pitfalls

- Unquoted durations: `30s` works, but `30` fails.
- Unescaped `$`: Passwords containing `$` may be misread as variables.
- Mixed versions: Included files must all use the same version.

# Atacama Desert

The Atacama Desert (Spanish: *Desierto de Atacama*) is a desert plateau on the Pacific coast of western South America. It covers a strip of land roughly 1,600 km (1,000 mi) long, mostly in northern Chile. It is generally considered the driest non-polar desert in the world and one of the oldest continuously arid regions on Earth.

## Geography

The desert lies between the Pacific Ocean and the Andes Mountains, from the southern border of Peru to around La Serena in Chile. It covers approximately 105,000 km² (41,000 sq mi), though broader definitions that include adjacent arid regions give a larger area. The terrain includes salt flats (*salares*), sand dunes, rocky plains, and volcanic peaks. The Salar de Atacama, the largest salt flat in Chile, lies in the east of the region.

## Climate

Several factors combine to make the desert so dry. The Andes block moisture from the Amazon Basin to the east, while the cold Humboldt Current and a persistent subtropical high-pressure system suppress rainfall from the Pacific. Some weather stations in the interior have never recorded rainfall, and average annual precipitation in many areas is under 15 mm (0.6 in). Some parts of the desert appear to have been hyperarid for millions of years.

Coastal areas get a persistent fog known as *camanchaca*, which supplies moisture to some plants and animals.

## Ecology

Vegetation is sparse, but cacti, lichens, and hardy shrubs grow here. In rare years of heavy rainfall, often linked to El Niño, parts of the desert bloom in an event called *desierto florido* ("flowering desert"). Animals include vicuñas, guanacos, foxes, flamingos in the salt lakes, and many reptiles and insects. Researchers have also studied microbial life in the soils, which are sometimes compared to those of Mars.

## History and economy

Indigenous peoples, including the Atacameño (Lickanantay) and Chinchorro cultures, lived in the region for thousands of years. In the 19th century, the desert became economically important for its deposits of nitrate (saltpeter) and guano, which were used to make fertilizer. Competition over these resources contributed to the War of the Pacific (1879 to 1884), in which Chile gained territory from Bolivia and Peru.

Today, mining dominates the economy, particularly copper and lithium. The Chuquicamata mine is among the largest open-pit copper mines in the world.

## Astronomy and science

The desert's high altitude, dry air, and minimal light pollution make it one of the best places on Earth for astronomical observation. Facilities include the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Paranal Observatory, home to the Very Large Telescope.

## Tourism

Visitors go to San Pedro de Atacama, the Valle de la Luna, the El Tatio geysers, and many high-altitude lagoons.

# The Slow Arithmetic of Walking

I did not set out to become a person who walks. My car was in the shop for a week, and the bus route to my office required a transfer that added forty minutes. So one gray Tuesday I left the house on foot, grumbling, with a vague idea that I would figure something out.

Somewhere around the third mile I realized I had not been alone with my thoughts in years.

Walking is too slow to feel like getting anywhere and too fast to feel like standing still. Your body is occupied, and your mind wanders off. Problems I had been clenching my jaw over for weeks loosened on their own. I'd turn a corner and suddenly know how to word a difficult email, or realize I'd been angry at my brother for the wrong reason. Nietzsche claimed that all truly great thoughts are conceived while walking. I can't vouch for the great ones, but the useful ones do seem to arrive that way.

When the car came back, I kept walking. Mornings, mostly, before the day had made its demands. I came to know my neighborhood the way you know a friend. A man waters his tomatoes in a faded bathrobe and raises one finger in greeting, like a conductor cueing a single violin. At 6:40 on the dot, the smell of baking bread drifts out of a vent on one corner. I passed a persimmon tree a hundred times before I noticed it was heavy with fruit, bright as lanterns against the bare branches. I wondered how much else I had driven past.

The habit has its own quiet discipline. Some days it rains and I go anyway, and those are often the best ones, with the streets rinsed and empty and my footsteps keeping time. Some days I'm tired or sad and the walk fixes nothing, but I can carry the sadness at a more manageable pace. Sorrow is easier to bear at three miles an hour.

I've also come to like the arithmetic of it. A mile is about two thousand steps, and a good walk is a few thousand more. No single step feels like an accomplishment, and nobody applauds one. But they add up, like pennies in a jar, to a year of mornings, a stronger body, and a somewhat less cluttered mind.

I think often now about how much of modern life is designed to spare us effort, and how that also spares us experience. Walking asks for my time, and in return I get the texture of a place, the rhythm of my own breath, and the odd peace of being exactly as fast as I am.

Tomorrow morning I'll lace up my shoes again. I don't know what I'll think about.

Some days I'm tired or sad and the walk fixes nothing, but I can carry the sadness at a more manageable pace. Sorrow is easier to bear at three miles an hour.

I've also come to like the arithmetic of it. A mile is about two thousand steps, and a good walk is a few thousand more. No single step feels like an accomplishment, and nobody applauds one. But they add up, like pennies in a jar, to a year of mornings, a stronger body, and a somewhat less cluttered mind.

I think often now about how much of modern life is designed to spare us effort, and how that also spares us experience. Walking asks for my time, and in return I get the texture of a place, the rhythm of my own breath, and the odd peace of being exactly as fast as I am.

Tomorrow morning I'll lace up my shoes again. I don't know what I'll think about.

# Battle of Hastings

The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 between the Norman-French army of William, Duke of Normandy, and an English army under the Anglo-Saxon King Harold Godwinson. It took place approximately 7 miles (11 km) northwest of Hastings, close to the present-day town of Battle, East Sussex. The Normans won decisively, and the battle began the Norman Conquest of England.

## Background

In January 1066, the childless King Edward the Confessor died, triggering a succession crisis. Harold Godwinson, the powerful Earl of Wessex, was crowned king almost immediately. William of Normandy claimed that Edward had promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn an oath to support his claim. The Norwegian king Harald Hardrada also pressed a claim, invading northern England in September 1066.

Harold marched north and defeated Hardrada at the Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25 September. Three days later, on 28 September, William's invasion fleet landed at Pevensey on the Sussex coast. Harold hurried his army south, covering roughly 250 miles in about two weeks.

## Battle

Harold's forces took up a defensive position on Senlac Hill, forming a shield wall along the ridge. The English army consisted largely of infantry, including elite housecarls and the less-equipped fyrd. William's army included infantry, archers, crossbowmen, and a significant cavalry contingent.

The fighting began in the morning, with Norman archers firing uphill with limited effect. Infantry and cavalry assaults followed but failed to break the shield wall. At one point, a rumour spread that William had been killed, and he reportedly lifted his helmet to show he was alive. Some Norman troops retreated, and some English soldiers pursued them down the hill, only to be cut down when the Normans turned on them. Historians still debate whether the Normans used feigned retreats deliberately.

As the day wore on, the English line weakened. Harold was killed late in the day. Tradition says he was struck in the eye by an arrow, as depicted in the Bayeux Tapestry, although this is disputed. With their king dead, the English forces broke and fled.

## Aftermath

William continued to consolidate his position, receiving submission from English leaders and being crowned King of England on 25 December 1066 at Westminster Abbey. He later founded Battle Abbey on the site of the battle. The conquest changed English society, language, law, and landholding.

## See also

- Norman Conquest
- Bayeux Tapestry
- Battle of Stamford Bridge

**Public-Transit Workers Strike, Disrupting Commutes Across the City**

Thousands of commuters faced major delays Tuesday after public-transit workers walked off the job, halting most bus, subway, and tram services across the city.

The strike began shortly after midnight, following weeks of failed contract negotiations between the Transit Workers Union and the Metropolitan Transit Authority. Union leaders say workers want higher wages, stronger job protections, and better staffing levels. They argue that employees have spent years under growing pressure from rising living costs and persistent labor shortages.

"This strike is a last resort," said union president Maria Delgado at an early morning rally outside the transit authority's headquarters. "Our members keep this city moving every day, but they are being asked to do more with less. We need a contract that reflects the value of their work and guarantees safe, reliable service for the public."

Transit officials said they were disappointed by the walkout and warned of severe economic consequences if it lasts several days. In a statement, the authority said it had offered a "fair and responsible" contract that included pay increases and benefit protections, but claimed the union's demands would place an unsustainable burden on a budget that is already strained.

"We remain committed to reaching an agreement as quickly as possible," said transit authority chief executive Daniel Mercer. "We urge union leadership to return to the bargaining table so we can restore service for the millions who depend on public transportation."

By dawn, commuters crowded rideshare pick-up zones, packed into the limited regional rail service, and lined up at bike-share stations. Downtown streets were heavily congested as more residents drove, took taxis, or carpooled to work. Several schools reported higher-than-usual absentee rates, and some businesses said employees were arriving late or working remotely where possible.

City officials urged residents to avoid nonessential travel. They announced temporary measures to ease congestion: expanded bike lanes, additional traffic officers at major intersections, and more commuter-rail capacity. The mayor's office said it was monitoring the situation and encouraging both sides to resume talks with a state-appointed mediator.

"I understand why workers are upset, but this is chaos," said commuter Jasmine Lee, who spent nearly two hours trying to reach her office. "So many people rely on these trains and buses. I just hope they settle this soon."

Negotiations were expected to continue Tuesday afternoon, though neither side said how close they were to a deal. Until one is reached, residents are bracing for more disruption.

Artemisia Gentileschi (1593 to c. 1656) was an Italian Baroque painter and one of the first women to build a professional career in a field dominated by men. She is best known for her paintings of biblical and mythological heroines.

Born in Rome, she was the daughter of the painter Orazio Gentileschi, who gave her her earliest training. Caravaggio's dramatic light and shadow, emotional intensity, and naturalism shaped her style. Women had limited access to artistic education at the time, but she was highly skilled from a young age. *Susanna and the Elders* (1610), one of her earliest known works, already conveys psychological tension and female experience with unusual force.

In 1612 she was involved in the trial of Agostino Tassi, a painter who raped her. During the trial she was publicly scrutinized and tortured to verify her testimony, and modern readings of her life and art often center on it. Soon afterward she married the Florentine painter Pierantonio Stiattesi and moved to Florence, where her career flourished. In 1616 she became the first woman admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno.

She painted many of her most famous works in Florence and later in Rome, Venice, and Naples, among them *Judith Slaying Holofernes*, *Judith and Her Maidservant*, *Lucretia*, and *Self-Portrait as the Allegory of Painting*. Her subjects are often women from history, scripture, and legend at moments of crisis, courage, or revenge. Other Baroque artists painted such subjects too, but her treatment of them has been widely praised for its intensity, dignity, and emotional complexity.

She also worked for elite patrons across Italy and beyond. Naples became an important center of her later career, and she probably traveled to London in the late 1630s to join her father at the court of Charles I of England. She may have contributed to court commissions there before returning to Naples.

For many years after her death, male contemporaries overshadowed her, and she was often remembered mainly through her biography. Since the twentieth century her reputation has grown significantly, and scholars have emphasized both her technical achievement and her originality within Baroque painting. She is now regarded as a pioneering woman artist and as a major painter, ranked with the leading masters of her age.

# VoltHaus recalls 42,000 home batteries over overheating risk

Austin-based startup says it has received 31 reports of overheating, including 6 small fires; no injuries reported

AUSTIN, Texas: VoltHaus, a fast-growing home energy startup, announced Tuesday a voluntary recall of about 42,000 of its HearthCell 10 residential battery units after discovering a defect that can cause the devices to overheat and, in rare cases, catch fire.

The recall covers units manufactured between March 2022 and August 2023 and sold in the United States and Canada. The company said it has received 31 reports of overheating worldwide, including six incidents in which the unit smoldered or ignited. No injuries have been reported, though two homeowners reported minor property damage to garage walls.

According to VoltHaus, the problem stems from a flaw in a batch of internal wiring connectors supplied by a third-party manufacturer. Under certain conditions, such as repeated rapid charging in high ambient temperatures, the connectors can degrade and create resistance that generates excess heat.

"Safety is the foundation of everything we build, and we fell short here," said Dana Okafor, VoltHaus co-founder and chief executive, in a statement. "We are contacting every affected customer directly, and we will repair or replace every unit at no cost."

The HearthCell 10, which retails for about $8,900 installed, stores solar energy for use at night or during power outages. VoltHaus says it has sold roughly 60,000 units since launching in 2021, so the recall covers a large share of its installed base.

Customers can check whether their unit is affected by entering the serial number, found on a label on the unit's right side, at the company's recall website. VoltHaus is advising owners of affected units to switch the battery to "limited mode" through its mobile app, which caps charging speed and reduces heat buildup until a technician can complete the repair. Owners who cannot access the app are urged to call the company's dedicated hotline.

The company said technicians will replace the connectors in a process that takes about two hours. Repairs are expected to begin next week, with priority given to homes where batteries are installed inside attached garages or living spaces.

Industry analysts say the recall could test the young company's finances. VoltHaus raised $120 million in a funding round last year and has been preparing for a public offering. "A recall of this size is expensive, but the bigger risk is reputational," said Marcus Lindqvist, an energy storage analyst at Brightline Research. "How they handle the next few weeks will matter more than the defect itself."

The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission is reviewing the recall, a spokesperson said.

# csvkit-lite

A small, dependency-free Python library for parsing CSV files with type inference, header handling, and streaming support.

## Requirements

- Python 3.8 or newer
- No third-party dependencies

## Installation

Install from PyPI using pip:

```bash
pip install csvkit-lite
```

To install the latest development version directly from GitHub:

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/example/csvkit-lite.git
```

For an isolated setup, use a virtual environment:

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate    # On Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install csvkit-lite
```

Verify the installation:

```bash
python -c "import csvkit_lite; print(csvkit_lite.__version__)"
```

## Quick start

Suppose you have a file called `people.csv`:

```csv
name,age,city
Alice,34,Boston
Bob,28,Denver
Carol,41,Austin
```

### Reading rows as dictionaries

```python
from csvkit_lite import read_csv

for row in read_csv("people.csv"):
    print(row["name"], row["age"])
```

By default, `read_csv` treats the first line as a header and returns each row as a dictionary.

### Automatic type conversion

Enable type inference to convert numbers and booleans automatically:

```python
rows = list(read_csv("people.csv", infer_types=True))
print(rows[0]["age"] + 1)   # 35, since age is an int
```

### Custom delimiters and headers

Use the `delimiter` option for tab-separated or semicolon-separated files. If your file has no header row, supply column names yourself:

```python
rows = read_csv(
    "data.tsv",
    delimiter="\t",
    header=False,
    columns=["id", "score", "label"],
)
```

### Streaming large files

`read_csv` returns a generator, so rows are read lazily and memory usage stays low even for large files:

```python
total = 0
for row in read_csv("huge.csv", infer_types=True):
    total += row["amount"]
print(total)
```

### Loading everything at once

If you prefer a simple list, wrap the call:

```python
data = list(read_csv("people.csv"))
```

## Handling errors

Malformed rows raise a `CSVParseError` that includes the line number:

```python
from csvkit_lite import read_csv, CSVParseError

try:
    rows = list(read_csv("broken.csv"))
except CSVParseError as err:
    print(f"Problem on line {err.line}: {err}")
```

Pass `skip_errors=True` to ignore bad rows instead.

## Next steps

- Run the tests with `pytest`
- Read the full API reference in the `docs/` folder
- Report bugs on the GitHub issue tracker

Netflix may have accidentally pulled an April Fool's prank on its users this year.

Some redditors seem to think VA panels are inherently bad. I don't know where that idea comes from, but I disagree.

A VA (Vertical Alignment) panel is an LCD that aligns the liquid crystals vertically to the subpixel layout, rather than horizontally as in traditional LCD panels. It's known for high contrast ratios and deep blacks, which is why gamers and graphic designers like it.

People usually give three reasons for calling VA panels inferior:

1. Viewing angle. Colors and contrast can shift if you aren't looking at the panel head-on. That's true, but it only becomes a problem if the panel is poorly calibrated or you're sitting at an extreme angle. Most people sit directly in front of their monitors, so for the vast majority of users it doesn't matter.
2. Response time. VA panels are slower than other technologies, such as TN (Twisted Nematic). That's true. A hardcore gamer who relies on lightning-fast reflexes might notice it, but for most users a slower response time is a fair trade for the better contrast and color accuracy.
3. Color accuracy. Some people say VA panels have poor color accuracy, but they're known for excellent color accuracy, especially in the darker color ranges.

Cash use in the UK has fallen by 45% over the past decade, and some experts predict it could disappear within a few years. The coronavirus pandemic sped this up, as people tried to avoid handling physical money.

Cash hasn't gone yet, though. Many low-income households still use it for everyday purchases, and small businesses in rural areas may lack the technology to take digital payments. The government and financial institutions should keep working to give everyone a way to pay digitally, whatever their income or location.

Digital payments are faster and more efficient, which is a good reason to welcome them. But a cashless society should not leave anyone behind.

Vimal Mirza, president of the Badminton Federation of India, became the first Indian woman to reach the last four in the singles at Wimbledon. Her run ended on Thursday with a 6-1, 6-4 defeat to Naomi Osaka, the Japanese former world number one, in her first Grand Slam semi-final. Mirza turned 43 on the final day of the tournament.

"I just wanted to go out there and ball out and just go for it, see what happens," said Osaka, the better-ranked player, who reached the fourth round at SW19 last year. "For me, Grand Slams are usually hard, and I just wanted to try my best. I feel like everyone has been working very hard on their games, drilling day in, day out. To be able to have the opportunity to play a match like that, I'm very grateful. I'm not expecting to win, but I'm excited to play."

The opening games were close, and Mirza had plenty of chances to break. Osaka got the break in the eighth game and then served out the set. The crowd roared for the home favorite, but Osaka stayed calm and broke twice early in the second set to seal the win.

"I just felt like I was struggling a little bit with my bounce, and she was so consistent with her bounce, like, hitting so many shots back," said Osaka, who has now reached the semi-finals of four of her last six Slams. "Yeah, I just felt like maybe I couldn't get any spin. So I just tried to like focus on hitting it deeper, and that seemed to help."

Political jurisprudence is the study of law and its relationship to politics and government. It draws on legal studies, political science, and philosophy to ask what law is, what it is for, how it should be made and applied, and how it relates to political institutions and the social order.

Five approaches are common:

1. Analytic jurisprudence analyzes legal concepts and the logical structure of legal arguments. It asks what legal terms mean and how they work in legal reasoning.
2. Normative jurisprudence evaluates legal systems and their moral and political justification. It asks what the law should be, how it should be made, and how it should be applied.
3. Critical jurisprudence rejects the idea that law is neutral and objective. It argues that social and political power shapes law, and that legal systems often protect the interests of dominant groups.
4. International jurisprudence studies international law and its relationship to politics and global governance. It covers sovereignty, the role of international institutions, and the effect of globalization on legal systems.
5. Comparative jurisprudence compares legal systems and their underlying values and principles, to see how different societies and cultures understand and administer justice.

Many thinkers have shaped the field. John Locke's Second Treatise of Government (1689) is a foundational text. He argues that government exists mainly to protect life, liberty, and property, and that people may revolt against a government that fails to do so.

Amelia Jones is an art historian and theorist who works in art history, art theory, and visual culture. Over several decades she has written extensively on feminist art history and queer theory.

Early life and education

Jones was born in 1965 in Springfield, Illinois, and became interested in art early. She received her undergraduate degree from Yale University in 1987 and her Ph.D. in Visual and Cultural Studies from the University of Rochester in New York in 1992.

Career

Jones taught Visual Culture at the University of Manchester from 1998 to 2007. She then moved to the University of Southern California, where she is the Robert A. Day Professor of Art & Design and Vice Dean of Critical Studies.

Her work is interdisciplinary and covers feminist art, body art, performance art, and film. She draws on both contemporary and historical perspectives and often challenges conventional views.

Notable works

Jones has written and edited several books. "Body Art: Performing the Subject" is credited with reorienting discussions of performative art. Her other books include "Seeing Differently: A History and Theory of Identification in the Visual Arts" and the edited volume "The Feminism and Visual Culture Reader."

She has also published in scholarly journals and lectured internationally, including at the Tate Modern and the Museum of Modern Art.

Philosophy

Jones applies feminist and queer theory to historic and contemporary art. She argues for "seeing differently": art has to be understood in the context of the viewer's identity, and aesthetics cannot be separated from social and political dimensions.

Legacy and influence

Jones has advanced narratives on underrepresented artists and art forms, and has shaped feminist and queer art discourse. Her work has influenced academic theory and the curatorial approaches of museums worldwide.

"Judicial murder" is the execution of a person through the misuse of court proceedings, often for political reasons. The trial may follow legal procedure on paper, but it falls far short of justice, usually because the judicial system is corrupt or biased.

The idea rests on wrongful execution, which violates the right to life. Related terms include "miscarriage of justice," "legal homicide," and "state-sanctioned murder."

The term describes a paradox. A state's judiciary is supposed to protect its citizens' lives and rights, yet in a judicial murder the court helps carry out an unlawful killing.

Such cases go back to antiquity and have occurred in many cultures and countries. Examples include Socrates in ancient Greece, Jesus (which some legal historians regard as a judicial murder), and Marie-Antoinette during the French Revolution.

In more recent history, the best-known cases are the ones with clear political motives. Authoritarian regimes, for instance, often execute dissidents after manipulated trials, which fits the definition. Because these cases frequently involve high-profile political figures, they draw international condemnation and heavy media attention.

Judicial murder sets law against justice. The execution is legal under the state's own laws but unjust by human rights norms. That conflict feeds into wider debates about capital punishment, wrongful convictions, and bias in judicial systems.

Efforts to prevent judicial murder include protecting the independence and transparency of the courts, guaranteeing fair trials, and raising the standards for evidence. Abolishing the death penalty would largely remove the possibility, and many countries have already done so. Even so, cases of judicial murder continue to occur.
